definitions.definition: Interception, as used in Section 46 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, refers to the lawful collection of wire, electronic, or oral communications by a competent authority under the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 or the Information Technology Act, 2000 or any other law for the time being in force, for use as evidence against an accused in proceedings related to offences under the Act. Such intercepted communication or evidence derived therefrom is admissible in court provided the accused is furnished with a copy of the competent authority's order at least ten days before trial, unless waived by the presiding judge.
definitions.plain_english: Interception means the lawful tapping or monitoring of phone calls, messages, emails, or spoken conversations by government authorities to gather evidence against terrorism suspects. This evidence can be used in court under UAPA, but the accused must be given a copy of the official order that permitted the interception at least ten days before the trial starts. The ten-day notice requirement can only be skipped if the judge decides it was not possible to provide it in time and the accused will not be unfairly harmed by the delay.
real_world_examples: The National Investigation Agency intercepts mobile phone calls and encrypted messaging app conversations of suspected Lashkar-e-Taiba operatives operating across the India-Pakistan border under authorisation from the competent authority under the Indian Telegraph Act, and submits transcripts as evidence during trial under UAPA.

Intelligence agencies intercept email communications between members of a designated terrorist organisation planning an attack in Mumbai, and the electronic records obtained are admitted as evidence in the special UAPA court after furnishing the accused with the interception order ten days before trial.

Police authorities, acting under the Information Technology Act, 2000, lawfully intercept online chat messages and VoIP calls of individuals suspected of financing a terrorist gang operating in Jammu & Kashmir, and the collected digital evidence is placed before the court in a UAPA prosecution.

The Delhi Police Special Cell intercepts satellite phone communications of a proclaimed offender coordinating a series of bomb blasts, and the recorded oral communication is admitted as evidence in the sessions court after compliance with the ten-day notice requirement under Section 46 of UAPA.

Security agencies intercept WhatsApp messages and wire transfers discussed over phone between recruiters of an unlawful association and new inductees in Kerala, and the intercepted content is used as primary evidence to establish conspiracy charges under UAPA before the designated court.
what_it_covers: Tapping of telephone or mobile phone calls (wire communication) by authorised agencies under the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 for collecting evidence in UAPA cases.
Interception of electronic communications such as emails, instant messages, social media chats, and VoIP calls under the Information Technology Act, 2000 in connection with terrorist activities.
Recording or monitoring of oral conversations (face-to-face or otherwise) captured through authorised surveillance devices by security agencies investigating terrorist acts or unlawful associations.
Evidence derived from intercepted communications, including transcripts, recordings, and analytical reports, when furnished to the accused with the requisite interception order copy.
Interception orders issued by a competent authority under any other law in force that authorises communication surveillance for national security or counter-terrorism purposes.
what_it_excludes: Unauthorised or illegal tapping of communications not backed by an order of the competent authority under the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, the IT Act, 2000, or any other applicable law, which cannot be admitted as evidence under Section 46.

Interception evidence where the accused has not been furnished with the competent authority's order at least ten days before trial and the judge has not waived this requirement, rendering such evidence inadmissible.
Evidence collected through private or unofficial surveillance by individuals or non-state actors, which does not qualify as lawful interception under the statutory framework referenced in Section 46.
Communications intercepted in proceedings unrelated to UAPA offences, such as purely civil disputes or ordinary criminal matters not involving terrorist activity or unlawful associations.
Voluntary disclosures or consensual recordings made without any official interception order, which are governed by general evidentiary rules rather than the admissibility framework of Section 46.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether evidence qualifies as lawfully obtained interception under Section 46 determines its admissibility in a UAPA trial, overriding the general exclusionary rules of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and thus directly affects whether an accused can be convicted on the basis of surveillance intelligence. Non-compliance with the ten-day notice requirement or failure to obtain a proper competent authority order can render intercepted evidence inadmissible, potentially collapsing the prosecution's case against a terrorist or member of an unlawful association.

definitions.definition: An 'investigating officer' means a gazetted officer of the Government endorsed with a copy of a prohibitory order under Section 7 for the purpose of investigation, or an officer investigating an offence committed under Chapter IV or Chapter VI who is empowered under Section 25 to seize or attach property representing proceeds of terrorism and to take all incidental investigative actions authorised under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: An investigating officer is a government officer (of gazetted rank) who is officially assigned to investigate matters under UAPA — either to look into funds being used by an unlawful association, or to investigate terrorism-related offences and seize property linked to terrorism. This officer has special legal powers such as entering premises, examining books, and seizing or attaching property. They must follow specific procedures laid down in the Act, including getting prior approvals and informing designated authorities within set time limits.
real_world_examples: A Superintendent of Police (a gazetted officer) is appointed to investigate an accused member of a banned organisation in Punjab; he is empowered to enter the accused's premises, examine bank accounts, and seize funds suspected to be used for the unlawful association's activities under Section 7.

An officer from the National Investigation Agency (NIA) investigating a terror financing case in Mumbai under Chapter VI has reason to believe certain real estate properties represent proceeds of terrorism; she obtains written approval from the Director General of Police and issues an attachment order under Section 25.

A gazetted officer of a State Police force in Jammu & Kashmir, endorsed with a prohibitory order copy, enters a hawala operator's office, examines transaction records, and makes inquiries about suspicious remittances suspected to be funding a terrorist organisation.

An NIA officer investigating a 2023 IED blast case in Manipur under Chapter IV seizes a large amount of cash from a suspect's residence under Section 25(5), suspecting it is intended to be used for a future terrorist act, and notifies the Designated Authority within 48 hours.

A gazetted officer of the Central Government endorsed under Section 7(2) investigates the books of a charitable trust in Hyderabad believed to be channelling moneys to an unlawful association, and makes inquiries from the trust's directors about the origin of suspicious transactions.
what_it_covers: A gazetted government officer endorsed with a copy of a prohibitory order under Section 7(2) to investigate funds of an unlawful association.

A police or NIA officer of appropriate rank investigating offences under Chapter IV (Punishment of Terrorist Activities) or Chapter VI (Terrorist Funds) who exercises seizure and attachment powers under Section 25.

An officer empowered to enter premises, examine books of accounts, search for moneys, securities or credits, and make inquiries from persons, officers, agents, or servants in connection with a UAPA investigation.
An officer who seizes or attaches property representing proceeds of terrorism after obtaining prior written approval of the Director General of Police of the relevant State.
An officer who seizes cash suspected of being intended for use in terrorism or forming part of the resources of a terrorist organisation under Section 25(5).
what_it_excludes: Non-gazetted or subordinate police officers who have not been formally endorsed or authorised under the relevant sections of UAPA to conduct investigations under Section 7 or Section 25.
Judicial officers, magistrates, or members of the Tribunal or Designated Authority who adjudicate or review investigative actions but do not themselves conduct field investigations under the Act.

Officers investigating offences outside the scope of Chapters IV and VI (such as offences under other chapters or under other laws) who have not been specifically authorised under UAPA for these purposes.
Private citizens, informants, or intelligence operatives who may gather information but do not hold the statutory power to seize, attach, or issue orders under UAPA.
Officers of foreign enforcement agencies or Interpol liaisons acting without a formal endorsement or authorisation under the Indian UAPA framework.
definitions.why_it_matters: The designation of a person as an 'investigating officer' under UAPA is the legal trigger that activates critical coercive powers — including the power to seize property, attach funds, enter premises, and examine records — without which such actions would be unlawful and liable to be set aside by courts. Failure to act through a properly designated investigating officer can invalidate seizures, attachment orders, and the entire chain of prosecution evidence in terrorism-related cases.

definitions.definition: Judicial custody, as used in Section 43D of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, refers to the custody of an accused person under the order and authority of a court, as distinct from police custody, wherein the accused is held in a correctional facility or lock-up under judicial supervision and remains subject to the court's jurisdiction pending investigation or trial. A person in judicial custody may be transferred back to police custody only upon the investigating officer filing an affidavit before the court stating specific reasons and explaining any delay in making such a request.
definitions.plain_english: Judicial custody means that an arrested person is kept in jail or a detention facility under the supervision and orders of a court, rather than being held at a police station. The police no longer have direct physical control over the person — instead, the court is responsible for ensuring the person's safekeeping. If investigators need the person back under police supervision for questioning, they must go back to court and explain exactly why, in writing.
real_world_examples: A person arrested in Mumbai for alleged involvement in a terrorist financing network is produced before a special NIA court after 30 days of police custody; the court remands them to judicial custody in Arthur Road Jail while the National Investigation Agency continues gathering evidence.

An accused charged under UAPA for alleged links to a banned organisation in Kashmir is held in Kot Bhalwal Jail under judicial custody after the initial police remand period expires; the investigating officer later files an affidavit before the court seeking a brief return to police custody to conduct a test identification parade.

A Delhi-based suspect arrested under UAPA for allegedly funding a proscribed terrorist organisation is remanded to Tihar Jail judicial custody after the maximum permissible police custody period ends; the trial court extends the overall detention period up to 180 days on the Public Prosecutor's report showing investigation progress.

Following the arrest of several accused in a Hyderabad-based terror module case, the NIA court places the accused in judicial custody at Cherlapally Central Prison; any subsequent request by police to take the accused for a site reconstruction exercise requires a sworn affidavit explaining the necessity and any delay.

In a case involving suspected ULFA cadres arrested in Assam, after the initial remand the accused are shifted from police lock-up to Guwahati Central Jail under judicial custody, and the court monitors all further extensions of detention under the modified timelines prescribed by Section 43D of UAPA.
what_it_covers: An accused person remanded to jail or a correctional facility by a court after the permissible police custody period has expired, pending completion of investigation under UAPA.
The period of detention during which the accused is under the court's authority and housed in a prison or state detention facility, not at a police station.

Continued detention of a UAPA accused beyond 90 days and up to 180 days where the court extends remand on the Public Prosecutor's progress report, with the accused remaining in judicial custody throughout.

The custodial status of an accused when an investigating officer seeks to obtain police custody from judicial custody, requiring the filing of an affidavit before the court explaining reasons and any delay.
what_it_excludes: Police custody, where the accused is physically held at a police station or remand home under the direct control of the investigating officer rather than the court.
Bail or release on personal bond, where the accused is no longer in any form of physical custody but subject to conditions imposed by the court.

Preventive detention under separate laws such as the National Security Act or Public Safety Act, which operates independently of the court-supervised remand process under the CrPC as modified by UAPA.
Custody of a witness or a person summoned by the court who has not been arrested as an accused under the Act.
Detention of a person in a hospital or medical facility for treatment, which does not constitute judicial custody in the statutory sense even if ordered by a court.
definitions.why_it_matters: The distinction between judicial custody and police custody under Section 43D is critical because it determines what procedural safeguards apply, including the requirement of a sworn affidavit before any transfer back to police custody, thereby protecting the accused from prolonged or arbitrary police interrogation. It also governs the computation of the extended detention periods (up to 180 days) permitted under UAPA and interacts directly with the bail restrictions under Section 43D(5), since an accused who is 'in custody' and fails to meet the stringent bail conditions must remain in judicial custody until trial.

definitions.definition: Any proceeding before the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Tribunal shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), and the Tribunal shall be deemed to be a civil court for the purposes of section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
definitions.plain_english: A 'judicial proceeding' under UAPA refers to any proceeding conducted before the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Tribunal that is treated as if it were a formal court proceeding. This means that giving false evidence or showing contempt before this Tribunal carries the same legal consequences as doing so in a regular court. Witnesses, documents, and conduct in such proceedings are all subject to the same rules and penalties as in an ordinary civil court trial.
real_world_examples: A witness summoned before the UAPA Tribunal to testify about the activities of a banned organisation like the Students Islamic Movement of India (SIMI) gives deliberately false testimony; that witness can be prosecuted under Section 193 IPC for perjury because the Tribunal's proceeding is a 'judicial proceeding'.

During a UAPA Tribunal inquiry into whether a particular organisation should be declared unlawful, a person produces a forged document as evidence; they can be charged under Section 228 IPC for intentional insult or interruption to a public servant sitting in judicial proceeding.

The Central Government constitutes a Tribunal to inquire into whether the Popular Front of India (PFI) should continue to be declared an unlawful association; all hearings before this Tribunal are treated as judicial proceedings, and any contemptuous behaviour by representatives of the organisation can attract penal consequences.

A government official is directed by the UAPA Tribunal to produce classified public records relating to a terrorist organisation; the requisition carries the authority of a civil court order because the proceeding is deemed a judicial proceeding, and non-compliance can result in legal action.

An advocate appearing before the UAPA Tribunal makes a statement on behalf of a banned militant outfit; since the proceeding is a judicial proceeding, false statements made by the advocate on oath are punishable under the Indian Penal Code just as they would be in a High Court.
what_it_covers: Any hearing, inquiry or proceeding conducted before the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Tribunal constituted under Section 5 of UAPA.
Examination of witnesses on oath before the Tribunal, making such testimony subject to perjury laws under Section 193 IPC.
Conduct and statements made before the Tribunal that may amount to intentional insult or interruption, attracting liability under Section 228 IPC.
Requisition of public records and issuance of commissions by the Tribunal, carrying the force of civil court orders.
Any complaint or action by the Tribunal against persons for offences committed in relation to its proceedings, governed by Section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the CrPC.
what_it_excludes: Proceedings before executive bodies or administrative authorities such as the Ministry of Home Affairs deciding to ban an organisation, which precede Tribunal adjudication and are not deemed judicial proceedings.
Internal deliberations, administrative decisions, or correspondence of the Tribunal that do not constitute a formal hearing or inquiry before it.
Police investigations, case diary preparations, or intelligence-gathering activities conducted by investigative officers under UAPA, which are investigative rather than judicial in nature.
Proceedings before a Review Committee constituted under UAPA, which is a separate body and not the Tribunal itself.

Proceedings in ordinary criminal courts, Sessions Courts, or High Courts under UAPA offences, which are already judicial proceedings by their own character and not by virtue of this deeming provision.

It also enables the Tribunal to invoke Section 195 CrPC and Chapter XXVI of the Code, empowering it to take cognizance of and deal with offences committed in relation to its proceedings, which it could not otherwise do as a non-court statutory body.

definitions.definition: Any instrument or substance capable of causing mass destruction includes unlicensed firearms, ammunition, explosives, or other instruments or substances whose use or deployment is capable of causing death, grievous injury, or significant damage to property on a large or indiscriminate scale, as contextually used in conjunction with biological, chemical, or high-explosive materials under Sections 10 and 23 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.
definitions.plain_english: Mass destruction refers to the potential of a weapon, substance, or instrument to kill, injure, or destroy property on a large scale in a single or coordinated act. This includes bombs, chemical agents, biological materials, or any explosive capable of causing widespread harm. The term is used to identify the especially dangerous nature of weapons possessed by members of unlawful associations or those aiding terrorists.
real_world_examples: A member of a banned organisation in Jammu & Kashmir found in possession of RDX explosives capable of destroying an entire building block — the substance qualifies as capable of mass destruction under Section 10.

A person linked to a terrorist gang in Maharashtra is apprehended with sarin gas canisters intended to be released in a crowded railway station — chemical warfare substances fall squarely within this definition under Section 23.

Operatives of a Maoist group in Chhattisgarh discovered with improvised explosive devices (IEDs) powerful enough to derail passenger trains, causing multiple casualties — such devices constitute instruments capable of mass destruction.

A suspect in Punjab is found with biological agents (anthrax spores) intended for contamination of a public water supply — biological substances of warfare capable of mass casualties are covered under Section 23 of UAPA.

Members of an unlawful association in Delhi are arrested with a cache of military-grade grenades and unlicensed automatic weapons, the combination of which is deemed capable of mass destruction when used collectively during a terrorist attack.
what_it_covers: Military-grade explosives such as RDX, PETN, or C-4 capable of destroying buildings or killing large numbers of people.
Chemical warfare substances including nerve agents (e.g., sarin, VX) or toxic industrial chemicals weaponised for deployment against civilians.
Biological agents such as anthrax, ricin, or plague bacteria prepared or possessed with intent to cause widespread casualties.
Radiological or nuclear materials that, if dispersed or detonated, could cause mass casualties and long-term environmental damage.
High-yield improvised explosive devices (IEDs) or vehicle-borne explosive devices (VBEDs) designed to cause indiscriminate casualties.
what_it_excludes: Conventional licensed firearms (e.g., a legally held hunting rifle or service revolver) not capable of causing large-scale indiscriminate harm.
Industrial chemicals or substances held for legitimate commercial or agricultural purposes with no weaponisation intent or capability.
Small-quantity crackers or pyrotechnic materials used for recreational or ceremonial purposes that do not carry destructive mass-casualty potential.
Standard police-issue batons, tear gas shells, or rubber bullets used for crowd control, which are not designed to cause mass destruction.
Medicinal or pharmaceutical substances, even if toxic in large doses, that are not configured or intended as weapons capable of mass casualties.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance or instrument qualifies as capable of 'mass destruction' is a critical threshold under Section 10(b) of UAPA — its presence elevates the offence from a two-year imprisonment to a mandatory minimum of five years up to life imprisonment, and to the death penalty if the act results in loss of human life. Under Section 23, possession of such materials with intent to aid a terrorist or terrorist organisation independently attracts a minimum five-year sentence up to life imprisonment, regardless of whether any attack actually occurs.

definitions.definition: The term 'member' is not expressly defined in Section 2 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967; however, as used in Section 20, a 'member' means any individual who belongs to, is associated with, or participates in a terrorist organisation, whether or not such membership is formal or acknowledged, and includes any person who professes to be a member of such an organisation.
definitions.plain_english: A 'member' under UAPA refers to any person who is part of a terrorist organisation — this can be someone who has formally joined, someone who actively participates in the group's activities, or even someone who publicly claims to belong to such an organisation. You do not need to have a membership card or formal enrolment; simply being associated with or functioning as part of the group can make you a member. Being a member of a terrorist organisation is itself a criminal offence under the Act.
real_world_examples: A person in Jammu & Kashmir who attends regular meetings of a banned terrorist organisation like Lashkar-e-Taiba, receives operational instructions, and carries out tasks assigned by its leadership is treated as a 'member' under Section 20 of UAPA.

An individual in Chhattisgarh who joins a Maoist (CPI-Maoist) cadre, undergoes ideological training, and participates in the organisation's activities — even if never directly involved in violence — is prosecutable as a member of a terrorist organisation.

A person in Tamil Nadu who openly proclaims on social media that he is an active member of a Schedule-listed terrorist outfit and solicits recruits on the organisation's behalf can be charged as a 'member' under UAPA Section 20.

A courier or logistical supporter in Delhi who is formally inducted into a terrorist organisation's network, receives payment from the outfit's funds, and regularly facilitates communication between operatives can be prosecuted as a member even without direct participation in a terrorist act.

A student in Hyderabad who attends the internal meetings of a banned organisation, takes an oath of allegiance to it, and distributes its literature under the organisation's direction qualifies as a 'member' regardless of whether violence has been committed.

An individual who is found in possession of membership documents, identity tokens, or encrypted communications identifying him as belonging to a listed terrorist organisation under the UAPA Schedule is presumed to be a 'member' for purposes of prosecution.
what_it_covers: Any individual formally inducted into a terrorist organisation listed in the Schedule of UAPA, regardless of their specific role or level of activity.
A person who professes or publicly claims to be a member of a terrorist organisation, even without formal documentation of membership.

An individual who functionally participates in the activities of a terrorist organisation — such as providing logistical support, attending meetings, or carrying out tasks — in a manner consistent with membership.
A person who has taken an oath of allegiance or undergone an initiation process into a terrorist organisation's structure.
An individual who receives remuneration, training, or operational directives from a terrorist organisation as part of their role within it.
what_it_excludes: A person who is merely acquainted with or related to a member of a terrorist organisation but has not participated in or associated themselves with the organisation's activities.
An informant, law enforcement officer, or intelligence agent who infiltrates a terrorist organisation for investigative purposes under authorisation of the State.

A journalist, researcher, or academic who interacts with members of a terrorist organisation solely for the purposes of reporting or scholarly study, without subscribing to its objectives or activities.
A person who was once a member but has formally renounced membership and surrendered to authorities under a rehabilitation or surrender scheme, to the extent protected by law.
Victims or hostages coerced into temporary cooperation with a terrorist organisation without voluntary association or intent to further its objectives.
definitions.why_it_matters: Being found to be a 'member' of a terrorist organisation under Section 20 of UAPA is itself a standalone criminal offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to imprisonment for life, without requiring proof of commission of a specific terrorist act. This definition determines whether an individual faces prosecution and the severe penal consequences under UAPA, including denial of bail under the stringent provisions of Section 43D.

definitions.definition: A metropolitan area means the metropolitan areas of Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Ahmedabad, and any other metropolitan area notified as such under sub-section (1) of section 8 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. These are designated urban jurisdictions within which a specific minimum rank of police officer — an Assistant Commissioner of Police — is required to investigate offences under Chapters IV and VI of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'metropolitan area' refers to large, officially designated cities in India — specifically Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, and Ahmedabad — as well as any other city that the government formally declares as a metropolitan area under the Criminal Procedure Code. In these cities, only a senior police officer of the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Police or above can investigate serious terrorism-related offences under UAPA. This ensures that investigations in major urban centres are handled by sufficiently senior and experienced officers.
real_world_examples: A UAPA terrorism case is registered at a Mumbai police station following a bomb blast; only an Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) or above from the Mumbai Police can lawfully investigate the offence under Chapters IV and VI of UAPA, not a Sub-Inspector or Inspector.

In Kolkata, intelligence agencies suspect an unlawful association is operating and financing terrorist activities; the investigation must be assigned to an officer of at least ACP rank within the Kolkata Police Commissioner's jurisdiction.

A suspected terrorist is arrested in Chennai for allegedly recruiting members for a banned organisation; the case file and investigation cannot be conducted by a lower-ranked officer such as a Deputy Inspector — it must be taken up by an ACP or equivalent.

The Central Government issues a gazette notification declaring Hyderabad as a metropolitan area under Section 8(1) of the CrPC; thereafter, any UAPA Chapter IV or VI offence investigated in Hyderabad must also be handled by an officer of ACP rank or above.

A joint UAPA investigation involving both Ahmedabad city police and a district police unit outside the metropolitan boundary requires the Ahmedabad portion to be handled by an ACP, while the non-metropolitan district portion can be handled by a Deputy Superintendent of Police.

A case involving counterfeit Indian currency linked to terrorist financing is registered in the metropolitan area of Mumbai; the investigating officer must hold at least the rank of ACP to ensure the investigation is legally valid and the evidence is not subsequently challenged on jurisdictional grounds.
what_it_covers: Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, and Ahmedabad as expressly named metropolitan areas where only an ACP-rank officer may investigate UAPA Chapter IV and VI offences.
Any other city or urban agglomeration officially notified as a metropolitan area by the Central or State Government under sub-section (1) of section 8 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

All police investigations into UAPA terrorism and unlawful association offences conducted within the territorial limits of a notified metropolitan area, regardless of the local police station involved.
Investigations by the city police commissioner's force within a metropolitan area where the suspect, offence, or evidence is located within that metropolitan boundary.
what_it_excludes: District towns, tehsil headquarters, or urban local body areas that have not been formally notified as metropolitan areas under Section 8(1) of the CrPC — investigations there are governed by the Deputy Superintendent of Police rank requirement.

Investigations conducted by the Delhi Special Police Establishment (CBI), which are separately governed under clause (a) of Section 43 regardless of whether the investigation takes place within a metropolitan area.
Rural or semi-urban areas falling outside the notified metropolitan limits even if they are adjacent to or part of the same district as a metropolitan city.
Investigations under Chapters other than IV and VI of UAPA, which are not subject to the rank restrictions specified in Section 43 for metropolitan areas.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a location qualifies as a 'metropolitan area' directly determines the minimum rank of police officer legally competent to investigate offences under Chapters IV and VI of UAPA — an ACP in metropolitan areas versus a Deputy Superintendent of Police elsewhere — and any investigation conducted by a lower-ranked officer within a metropolitan area may be legally invalid, potentially compromising prosecution. This classification thus acts as a gatekeeping mechanism ensuring accountability and seniority in the investigation of serious terrorism-related offences in India's largest cities.

definitions.definition: As used in the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 'moneys' refers to any sum of money in any currency, form or denomination, including cash and liquid monetary assets, that is in the custody of any person and which is being used or is intended to be used for the purposes of an unlawful association, or in respect of which a prohibitory order has been issued by the Central Government under Section 7.
definitions.plain_english: The term 'moneys' means actual money — whether in cash or any other monetary form — that belongs to or is connected with a banned (unlawful) organisation. This includes any money a person is holding that is being used, or is planned to be used, to support that banned group. The government can freeze such money and prohibit anyone from using or transferring it.
real_world_examples: A hawala operator in Delhi receives a cash transfer equivalent to ₹50 lakhs on behalf of a designated unlawful organisation; these funds constitute 'moneys' subject to a Central Government prohibitory order under Section 7.

A sympathiser of a banned Maoist organisation in Chhattisgarh collects monthly contributions from local businessmen and holds them in a gunny bag at his residence; such collected cash amounts are 'moneys' as used in Section 7 and attract penal liability under Section 11.

A bank account holder in Mumbai is found to be receiving regular wire transfers from an overseas Khalistani separatist network designated as an unlawful association; the balances and credits flowing through that account qualify as 'moneys' under UAPA.

A treasurer of a proscribed organisation in Jammu & Kashmir holds ₹10 lakhs in cash collected as membership dues intended for funding the group's activities; the Central Government can prohibit him from disbursing these moneys under Section 7(1).

A shopkeeper in Hyderabad keeps currency notes handed to him by members of a banned outfit with instructions to pay them to certain individuals later; these notes constitute 'moneys' and any dealing in contravention of a prohibitory order makes him liable under Section 11.
what_it_covers: Physical cash in Indian rupees or any foreign currency held by a person on behalf of or for the benefit of an unlawful association.
Liquid monetary balances or deposits in bank accounts that are being used or are intended to be used for the purposes of a proscribed organisation.
Any sum of money that comes into a person's custody after a prohibitory order is issued, where such money is connected to the unlawful association's activities.
Monetary contributions, collections or donations received by an individual for onward transmission to a banned organisation.
Money held by a corporation, company or bank that has been identified as linked to or intended for use by an unlawful association.
what_it_excludes: Securities (such as bonds, shares or acknowledgment documents for legal liability to pay money), which are separately enumerated alongside 'moneys' in Sections 7 and 11 as a distinct category.
Credits, which are also separately listed as a standalone category distinct from 'moneys' in the same sections, covering book-entry obligations and receivables.
Property in non-monetary form such as land, buildings, vehicles or goods, which falls under the broader definition of 'property' rather than 'moneys' as used in these sections.
Money that has no connection whatsoever to an unlawful association and is established by a court to be held for legitimate personal or business purposes.
Funds held by a bona fide transferee who received money without knowledge of its link to an unlawful association and can establish that fact before the District Judge.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a sum qualifies as 'moneys' under Sections 7 and 11 determines whether the Central Government can issue a prohibitory order freezing it and whether any person who deals with it in contravention of that order faces criminal punishment of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine, and an additional recovery fine equal to the amount contravened; it thus directly triggers both the prohibition regime and penal liability under UAPA.

definitions.definition: A notification published in the Official Gazette by the Central Government or State Government, as the context requires, for the purpose of giving formal public notice of an official act, order, or declaration made under the provisions of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'notification' under UAPA is an official announcement published in the Government Gazette — India's official public journal — by the Central or State Government. It is the formal legal mechanism by which the government makes its decisions binding on the public. Think of it as an official notice board posting that has the force of law once published.
real_world_examples: The Ministry of Home Affairs publishes a notification in the Official Gazette declaring a particular organization, such as a separatist group operating in Jammu & Kashmir, as an unlawful association under Section 3 of UAPA.

The Central Government issues a notification in the Official Gazette specifying a Joint Secretary-rank officer as the 'Designated Authority' empowered to exercise powers under UAPA in a particular state.

When the government decides to add a new terrorist organization to the Schedule of UAPA, it does so by publishing a notification in the Official Gazette, making the listing legally effective from the date of publication.
A State Government issues a notification under UAPA specifying a Secretary-level officer as its Designated Authority for handling unlawful association matters within its territory.

The Central Government notifies an amendment to the Prevention and Suppression of Terrorism Order via a gazette notification, updating the list of designated entities in line with UN Security Council Resolutions.
what_it_covers: A gazette notification declaring an association as an unlawful association under Section 3 of UAPA.
A notification specifying the Designated Authority — Central or State Government officer — empowered to act under the Act.
Any official public order issued by the Central or State Government under UAPA that must be communicated to the public with legal effect.
Notifications adding or modifying entries in the Schedule of terrorist organisations.
what_it_excludes: Informal government circulars or press releases that are not published in the Official Gazette and do not carry statutory force.
Internal administrative communications or office memoranda between government departments that are not intended for public notice.
Oral orders or directions issued by government officers even if issued under UAPA, as a notification must be in written and published form.
Court orders or judicial pronouncements, which are distinct from executive notifications and are governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure.
definitions.why_it_matters: The issuance of a valid notification is a jurisdictional prerequisite for several critical actions under UAPA — most notably, the declaration of an association as unlawful under Section 3 and the appointment of a Designated Authority — meaning that without a proper gazette notification, such declarations and appointments have no legal force and any consequential actions (bans, prosecutions, seizures) may be void. Whether a notification has been duly published directly determines the legality of government action and the rights of individuals or associations affected by it.

definitions.definition: A 'notified place' is any place notified by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette under sub-section (1) of section 8, being a place which in the opinion of the Central Government is used for the purpose of an unlawful association in respect of which a notification under section 3 has become effective. For the purposes of section 8, 'place' includes a house or building, or part thereof, or a tent or vessel.
definitions.plain_english: A 'notified place' is a location — such as a building, house, tent, or boat — that the Central Government officially declares (by publishing a notice in the Official Gazette) to be used by a banned organisation. Once a place is declared a notified place, the government gains special powers over it: it can restrict who enters, search people, list and freeze items found there, and remove unauthorised persons. Essentially, it is a government-flagged location linked to an illegal group.
real_world_examples: An office building in Srinagar used as a coordination hub by a banned militant organisation is declared a notified place by the Central Government under section 8, allowing the District Magistrate to restrict entry and inventory all equipment found inside.

A madrasa in Hyderabad identified as a recruitment and training centre for a proscribed terrorist outfit is notified under section 8, enabling authorities to search all persons entering the premises and prohibit use of computers and communication devices found there.

A warehouse in Mumbai used by a declared unlawful association to store funds, literature, and arms is published as a notified place in the Official Gazette, triggering restrictions on entry for non-residents and allowing police to search any individual seeking to enter.

A river vessel operating along the Kerala coast, used by a banned separatist group for meetings and logistics, is notified as a notified place, granting authorities the power to board, search passengers, and remove unauthorised persons from the vessel.

A residential compound in Delhi used as the administrative headquarters of a proscribed organisation is declared a notified place, after which the District Magistrate lists all movable property found on the premises and prohibits their use without written authorisation.
what_it_covers: A house or building, or any part thereof, used for the purposes of a declared unlawful association and notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette.
A tent used as a temporary base or meeting point by members of a proscribed organisation and officially notified under section 8(1).
A vessel (such as a boat or ship) used by a banned organisation for operations, communication, or logistics, and notified accordingly.
Any premises in respect of which the Central Government forms an opinion — even if not conclusively proved — that it is being used for the purpose of the unlawful association.
A place that was previously used by the unlawful association, provided the Central Government's opinion at the time of notification covers its use for such purposes.
what_it_excludes: Places that have not been formally notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette, even if they are suspected of being used by a banned group.
Premises of near relatives of residents of the notified place, who retain a right of access under the proviso to section 8(4) and are not subject to the entry restriction order.

Wearing-apparel, cooking vessels, beds and beddings, tools of artisans, implements of husbandry, cattle, grain, food-stuffs and articles of trivial nature found in the place, which are excluded from the list of movable properties subject to prohibitory orders under section 8(2).
A location associated with a suspected but not yet formally declared unlawful association — the notification under section 3 must have become effective before a notified place can be declared.
Private residences or commercial premises with no connection to a declared unlawful association, regardless of proximity to a notified place.
definitions.why_it_matters: Once a place is declared a 'notified place', it triggers a cascade of legal consequences: the District Magistrate acquires powers to inventory and freeze movable property, restrict and regulate entry, authorise searches of persons, and remove trespassers — any contravention of orders made in respect of a notified place attracts criminal liability under section 12, including imprisonment of up to one year and a fine. The designation is therefore the foundational trigger for all enforcement, search, entry-restriction, and penal provisions under sections 8 and 12 of UAPA.

definitions.definition: The term 'offence' is not separately defined in Section 2 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967; however, as used in the Act and specifically in Section 22B, it refers to any act or omission constituting a punishable violation under the provisions of this Act, including unlawful activities, terrorist acts, and offences relating to terrorist organisations, terrorist funding, and related activities. It encompasses every act or omission contrary to the provisions of this Act for which a person may be tried and held guilty before a competent court.
definitions.plain_english: An 'offence' under UAPA means any action or failure to act that breaks the rules set out in this law — such as committing a terrorist act, being a member of a banned organisation, raising funds for terrorism, or supporting unlawful activities. If a person does something the UAPA prohibits (or fails to do something the UAPA requires), that is an offence. The person can be arrested, tried, and punished for it.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai who raises funds and transfers money to a designated terrorist organisation such as Lashkar-e-Taiba, knowing it will be used for terrorist activities, commits an offence under UAPA.

Members of a banned organisation in Manipur who continue to participate in its activities, attend meetings, and distribute propaganda after the organisation has been declared unlawful commit an offence under UAPA.

An individual in Delhi who plants explosives in a public market intending to cause widespread death and damage to government property commits a terrorist act, which constitutes an offence punishable under UAPA.

A person in Punjab who harbours and conceals a proclaimed offender known to be a terrorist, providing shelter and logistical support to help that individual evade arrest, commits an offence under Section 22B of UAPA.
A financier in Hyderabad who knowingly facilitates the transfer of proceeds of terrorism through hawala channels to fund recruitment and training of terrorists commits a serious offence under UAPA.
An office-bearer of a terrorist gang in Jammu & Kashmir who recruits youth by distributing literature promoting secession and organising training camps commits an offence under UAPA.
what_it_covers: Committing a terrorist act as defined under Section 15 of the Act, including bombings, assassinations, or acts intended to threaten the unity and integrity of India.
Raising, collecting, or transferring funds for the purpose of supporting a terrorist act, terrorist gang, or terrorist organisation.
Being a member, supporter, or office-bearer of a declared unlawful association or terrorist organisation and continuing activities in its furtherance.
Harbouring or concealing any person who has committed an offence under the Act or is a proclaimed offender.
Organising or attending camps for training in terrorism or recruiting individuals into terrorist organisations.
Any act or omission committed by an Indian citizen outside India that would constitute an offence under UAPA if committed within India.
what_it_excludes: Acts or omissions that are punishable exclusively under other statutes such as the Indian Penal Code or Arms Act, unless they independently satisfy the elements of an offence under UAPA.
Bona fide journalistic reporting, academic research, or lawful advocacy on issues related to unlawful organisations, unless such activity crosses into active support or incitement.

Acts committed without the requisite mens rea (criminal intention or knowledge) required under specific provisions of UAPA, such as unknowing possession of materials later found connected to terrorism.
Actions of a bona fide transferee who acquires property without knowledge that it constitutes proceeds of terrorism, as such persons are protected under the Act.
Acts committed by persons not falling within the jurisdiction of UAPA, such as foreign nationals on foreign soil with no connection to India, ships, or aircraft registered in India.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a particular act constitutes an 'offence' under UAPA determines whether a person can be arrested without a warrant by a police officer, detained for extended periods, tried before a Special Court, and subjected to stringent bail conditions under Section 43D. It also triggers the State's power to attach and forfeit property linked to the offence and activates the enhanced punishments prescribed across Chapters IV, V, and VI of the Act.

definitions.definition: An 'offence under this Act' refers to any act or omission that is declared punishable under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, including but not limited to offences relating to unlawful activities, terrorist acts, membership of terrorist organisations, holding of proceeds of terrorism, and failure to furnish information as required under this Act, committed by any person, company, society, or trust.
definitions.plain_english: This term refers to any crime or wrongdoing that is specifically made punishable under the UAPA law itself. It covers acts like joining a terrorist group, committing a terrorist attack, handling money linked to terrorism, or refusing to give information to investigators when legally required. Only actions that this specific law defines as criminal count as an 'offence under this Act' — not crimes under other laws like the IPC.
real_world_examples: A person in Mumbai who knowingly provides funds to a designated terrorist organisation such as Lashkar-e-Taiba is committing an offence under this Act, enabling investigators under Section 43A to arrest them and search their premises.

A company director in Delhi whose firm is found to have channelled money to a terrorist gang, with the director's knowledge and connivance, commits an offence under this Act under Section 22A, making the director personally liable alongside the company.

A bank manager in Hyderabad who, upon being formally required under Section 43F by an investigating officer to furnish account details of a suspected terrorist, deliberately provides false information, commits an offence under sub-section (2) of Section 43F, punishable with imprisonment up to three years.

A trust registered in Chennai whose office-bearers are found to have used trust funds for financing a terrorist camp in a conflict zone commits an offence under this Act, triggering liability under Section 22B for all responsible office-bearers and the settlor.

A member of a proscribed unlawful association in Jammu & Kashmir who participates in the association's activities after it has been notified commits an offence under this Act, authorising an empowered officer under Section 43A to arrest and search based on information received in writing.
what_it_covers: Any terrorist act as defined under UAPA, including bomb blasts, assassinations, or disruption of essential services committed with terrorist intent.
Membership in, or support of, a declared terrorist organisation or unlawful association, including fundraising, recruitment, or training activities.
Holding, transferring, or using illegally acquired property or proceeds of terrorism in contravention of the Act.
Deliberate failure or refusal to furnish information required by an investigating officer under Section 43F, or knowingly furnishing false information.
Acts committed by companies, societies, or trusts and their responsible officers that constitute violations of the Act's provisions under Sections 22A and 22B.
what_it_excludes: Offences under other statutes such as the Indian Penal Code, Arms Act, or NDPS Act, even if they occur alongside a UAPA-related investigation, unless separately charged under UAPA provisions.
Civil wrongs, tortious acts, or contractual breaches that may tangentially involve a terrorist context but are not specifically made punishable under UAPA.

Acts committed by ex-officio government representatives on the governing board of a society or trust in their official capacity, who are expressly excluded from the definition of 'director' under Section 22B.
Offences committed by persons who prove they had no knowledge of the wrongdoing and had exercised reasonable care to prevent it, as provided in the provisos to Sections 22A and 22B.

Preliminary preparatory acts that do not yet constitute a design to commit or actual commission of a punishable act as defined under UAPA, such as mere association with individuals without any unlawful activity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as an 'offence under this Act' directly determines whether the special powers of arrest, search, and seizure under Section 43A can be lawfully exercised and whether the obligation to furnish information under Section 43F is triggered; it also governs the applicability of corporate and institutional criminal liability under Sections 22A and 22B, and the summary trial procedure under Section 43F(3).

definitions.definition: An office-bearer, as used in the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, refers to any person who holds a position of authority, management, or leadership in an association, including but not limited to its principal officers, and upon whom notices and communications regarding the declaration of unlawfulness of such association may be served. The term encompasses those who represent, manage, or act on behalf of the association in an official capacity.
definitions.plain_english: An office-bearer is someone who holds a formal leadership or management role in an organisation or association — for example, a president, secretary, treasurer, or any other named official. Under UAPA, these are the people who can be contacted on behalf of the organisation when the government takes legal action against it. They are treated as the official face or representative of the association and can be required to respond to legal proceedings.
real_world_examples: The president of a banned outfit such as the Students Islamic Movement of India (SIMI) who signs official communications and leads meetings qualifies as an office-bearer and can be served notice by the Tribunal under Section 4.

A treasurer of an organisation declared unlawful under UAPA, who manages the association's funds and bank accounts in Maharashtra, is an office-bearer and can be summoned to provide information to the Tribunal during the adjudication inquiry.

The general secretary of a Maoist front organisation operating in Chhattisgarh, responsible for coordinating activities and maintaining records, would be considered an office-bearer and is liable to be served a copy of the notification declaring the association unlawful.

The joint convener of a separatist group in Jammu & Kashmir who publicly represents the association at press conferences and signs membership documents is an office-bearer for the purposes of Section 4 proceedings before the Tribunal.

A district-level coordinator of a banned outfit in Punjab who officially recruits members and organises activities on behalf of the association's central body would be treated as an office-bearer and required to show cause before the Tribunal.
what_it_covers: The president, secretary, treasurer, or any named functionary who holds a formal post within the association's organisational structure.
A person who officially represents the association in dealings with third parties, the government, or the public, even if their title is informal such as 'coordinator' or 'convener'.
Any individual who is recognised by the association's constitution, rules, or practice as having authority to act, manage affairs, or make decisions on behalf of the association.
A principal office-bearer who is identified and served a copy of the notification under Section 3 for the purposes of adjudication before the Tribunal under Section 4.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary members of the association who do not hold any formal or functional leadership role and have no authority to act on behalf of the association.
Passive sympathisers or supporters of the association who are not officially affiliated with or registered as part of its organisational hierarchy.
Third-party individuals such as lawyers, accountants, or consultants engaged by the association on a professional basis without any internal governance role.
Government-appointed administrators or nominees who may oversee the association's affairs following a legal order but are not part of the association's own structure.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as an office-bearer determines whether they can be served notice, required to show cause, and summoned to provide information to the Tribunal during adjudication proceedings under Section 4 of UAPA; failure to respond or participation in a declared unlawful association as an office-bearer can expose the individual to prosecution, arrest, and punishment under the Act. It also determines the validity of service of the government's notification, which is a prerequisite for the declaration of an association as unlawful taking effect.

definitions.definition: "person" includes— an individual, a company, a firm, an organisation or an association of persons or a body of individuals, whether incorporated or not, every artificial juridical person, not falling within any of the preceding sub-clauses, and any agency, office or branch owned or controlled by any person falling within any of the preceding sub-clauses.
definitions.plain_english: Under UAPA, a 'person' is not limited to a human being. It covers a very wide range of entities including individual humans, companies, firms, unregistered groups, and any legal entity recognized by law. Even an office, agency, or branch that is owned or controlled by any of these entities is treated as a 'person' under this law.
real_world_examples: A private limited company registered in Mumbai that allegedly provides financial support to a banned terrorist organisation can be prosecuted as a 'person' under UAPA and its accounts can be frozen or its proceeds of terrorism seized.

An unregistered student association in a Delhi university that collectively undertakes activities promoting secession of a part of Indian territory qualifies as a 'person' and can be proceeded against under the Act.

A sole individual, such as a suspected lone-wolf terrorist arrested in Jammu, is a 'person' under the Act and can be charged with terrorist acts, with special procedural rules for bail and investigation applying to him personally.

A foreign NGO's India branch office in Bengaluru, controlled by a parent body abroad that is listed as a terrorist organisation, is treated as a 'person' under UAPA since it is a branch owned or controlled by an entity falling within the definition.

A registered partnership firm operating a hawala network in Hyderabad and channelling funds to a terrorist gang is a 'person' whose property constituting proceeds of terrorism can be attached and forfeited under the Act.

A State-owned public sector undertaking that is found to have unknowingly transferred funds to a terrorist organisation through a fraudulent contract would be examined as a 'person' for purposes of proceeds of terrorism provisions under UAPA.
what_it_covers: A natural individual human being, whether an Indian citizen, foreign national, or stateless person.
A company incorporated under the Companies Act, a limited liability partnership, or any other registered firm.
An unregistered association or body of individuals such as an informal group, trust, or community organisation not formally incorporated.
Every artificial juridical person recognised by law, such as a university, statutory body, or local authority, not otherwise covered.
Any agency, office, or branch that is owned or controlled by any individual, company, firm, organisation, or juridical person falling within the definition.
what_it_excludes: Entities that are entirely independent of and not controlled by any individual, company, firm, or organisation — a purely theoretical exclusion since all entities trace back to some controller.

The Central Government and State Governments in their sovereign capacity are not typically prosecuted as 'persons' liable under UAPA's offence provisions, though the definition does not expressly exclude them.
A deceased individual no longer capable of being a subject of prosecution, as the term contemplates living or subsisting legal entities capable of criminal or civil liability.
Animals, natural objects, or inanimate things that have not been accorded juridical personality under any law are not covered by the definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: The scope of 'person' directly determines who can be prosecuted for terrorist acts, whose property can be attached as proceeds of terrorism, and who can be designated as a terrorist under UAPA — a narrow reading would shield corporate or organisational structures used to finance terrorism, while the broad inclusive definition ensures that entities at every level of a terrorist network face legal consequences. Obligations such as freezing of funds, forfeiture of property, and sanctions under the Act are all triggered by whether the relevant entity qualifies as a 'person'.

definitions.definition: A 'place' means any house, room, premises, vehicle, vessel, aircraft or any other location which is used for the purpose of an unlawful association, and which the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, notify as a notified place under Section 8 of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: A 'place' under UAPA refers to any physical location — such as a building, room, vehicle, or other premises — that is being used by a banned or unlawful organisation for its activities. Once the government identifies and officially notifies such a location, it becomes subject to search, seizure, and other legal actions. Essentially, it is any spot where an unlawful association operates, meets, stores materials, or carries out its work.
real_world_examples: A rented apartment in Delhi used by members of a banned terrorist outfit as a safe house for planning activities would be a 'place' notifiable under Section 8.
An office building in Mumbai used as a front business by a proscribed separatist organisation to raise funds and recruit members would qualify as a notifiable 'place'.
A warehouse in Punjab used by an unlawful association to store arms, pamphlets, or funds connected to the organisation's activities would be covered as a 'place' under UAPA.
A vehicle or van being regularly used by members of a banned group to transport materials, hold meetings, or coordinate operations could be treated as a 'place' under this section.

A religious or community hall in Hyderabad being regularly used for meetings and indoctrination sessions by a notified unlawful organisation would fall within the definition of a 'place' under Section 8.
semantic_tags: physical location used by unlawful association
movable property list in notified place
what_it_covers: Any house, room, or building used as a base of operations, meeting point, or storage facility by a declared unlawful association.
Vehicles, vessels, or aircraft regularly used by members of an unlawful association for coordination, transportation of materials, or communication.
Commercial premises, offices, or warehouses serving as front operations or logistical hubs for a banned organisation.
Temporary locations such as rented halls or guesthouses where an unlawful association holds meetings or training sessions.
Any location, regardless of ownership, that is demonstrably used for the purpose of furthering the activities of an unlawful association.
what_it_excludes: A location merely owned by a member of an unlawful association but not actually used for the purposes of that association's activities.
Private residences or personal property of individuals who have no connection to the unlawful association, even if located near a notified place.
Places used exclusively for lawful purposes even if incidentally connected to a person who is also a member of a banned organisation.
Virtual or digital spaces such as online platforms, websites, or chat groups, which are not physical locations and thus fall outside the scope of 'place' under Section 8.
Places that were previously used by an unlawful association but have no current connection to its activities at the time of notification.
definitions.why_it_matters: Once the Central Government notifies a 'place' under Section 8, it triggers a mandatory process by the District Magistrate to list all movable properties found therein, authorises search and seizure operations, and enables forfeiture of assets connected to the unlawful association. Failure to recognise a location as a 'place' under this provision would prevent the State from conducting lawful entry, seizure, and proceedings against the property and persons associated with the unlawful association at that location.

definitions.definition: 'Proceeds of terrorism' means all kinds of properties which have been derived or obtained from commission of any terrorist act or have been acquired through funds traceable to a terrorist act, irrespective of person in whose name such proceeds are standing or in whose possession they are found; or any property which is being used, or is intended to be used, for a terrorist act or for the purpose of an individual terrorist or a terrorist gang or a terrorist organisation. For the purposes of the Act, it is declared that the expression 'proceeds of terrorism' includes any property intended to be used for terrorism.
definitions.plain_english: Proceeds of terrorism refers to any money, property, or assets that came from a terrorist attack or were bought using money linked to terrorism, no matter who officially owns them or who is holding them. It also includes any property that is being used for terrorism or is meant to be used for terrorism in the future. Essentially, it covers both the financial fruits of past terrorist acts and resources earmarked for future ones.
real_world_examples: A flat in Mumbai purchased using hawala money funnelled by a designated terrorist organisation to finance its operatives in India would constitute proceeds of terrorism, even if the flat is registered in the name of a relative of the operative.

Cash collected through extortion by a Maoist group in Jharkhand and deposited in a bank account, later used to buy weapons and explosives, qualifies as proceeds of terrorism as the funds are traceable to terrorist activity.

A vehicle owned by a sympathiser in Punjab that is regularly used to transport members of a proscribed terrorist gang to carry out attacks is considered proceeds of terrorism because it is being used for terrorist acts.

Foreign currency wire-transferred to a sleeper cell in Hyderabad by an overseas terrorist organisation, and held in a cryptocurrency wallet awaiting deployment for a planned attack, constitutes proceeds of terrorism as property intended to be used for a terrorist act.

A warehouse in Delhi stocked with chemicals intended for making improvised explosive devices, funded through donations collected under the guise of charity by a banned organisation, falls within the definition of proceeds of terrorism.

Agricultural land in Kashmir acquired by a terrorist organisation using ransom money obtained from kidnapping a public functionary is proceeds of terrorism, regardless of the benami name in which it is registered.
what_it_covers: Property directly derived from the commission of a terrorist act, such as ransom money paid to a terrorist gang following a kidnapping.
Assets acquired through funds traceable to a terrorist act, including real estate, vehicles, or bank balances purchased with terrorist financing, regardless of who holds or owns them.

Property currently being used to facilitate a terrorist act or to support an individual terrorist, terrorist gang, or terrorist organisation, such as safe houses, vehicles, or communication equipment.
Property intended to be used in a future terrorist act, even if no terrorist act has yet been committed, such as stockpiled cash or materials earmarked for an attack.
Proceeds held in the name of or in the possession of a third party, including relatives or associates of a terrorist, where the underlying funds are traceable to terrorism.
what_it_excludes: Legitimately earned property or income of an individual that has no traceable connection, direct or indirect, to any terrorist act, terrorist fund, or terrorist organisation.
Property held by a bona fide transferee who acquired it for adequate consideration without knowledge of its terrorist origin, to the extent such a transferee's rights are protected under the Act.
Proceeds or assets arising from ordinary criminal offences not amounting to a 'terrorist act' as defined under Section 15 of UAPA, such as routine robbery or fraud with no terrorist nexus.
Property that is merely owned by or associated with a person who happens to be a member of an unlawful association, but which was not derived from, used for, or intended for any terrorist act.
Humanitarian aid or funds received by legitimate charitable organisations that are not banned and have no operational link to any terrorist organisation, terrorist gang, or individual terrorist.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether property qualifies as 'proceeds of terrorism' directly determines whether it is subject to seizure, attachment, and forfeiture under Chapters IV and V of UAPA, and whether knowingly holding such property constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment up to life under Section 21. It also triggers the prohibition on dealing with such proceeds under Sections 25, 26, and 27, making any transfer, concealment, or use of such property a separate punishable offence.

definitions.definition: A 'proclaimed offender' under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act refers to a person accused of an offence under Chapter IV or Chapter VI who has been declared a proclaimed offender by a competent court, typically where such person has absconded or evaded the process of law, thereby preventing the conclusion of trial proceedings against them.
definitions.plain_english: A proclaimed offender is someone who has been formally declared by a court as a person who is deliberately evading arrest or trial, usually by going into hiding or fleeing the country. Under UAPA, this status specifically applies to individuals accused of terrorism-related or unlawful activity offences. When a person is declared a proclaimed offender, the court can proceed to confiscate their property even without completing the full trial.
real_world_examples: A suspected terrorist from a banned organisation who was chargesheeted for funding terrorist activities under Chapter VI of UAPA but fled to a neighbouring country before the trial could begin is declared a proclaimed offender by the special court in Mumbai, enabling attachment and confiscation of his properties in Maharashtra.

A member of a designated terrorist organisation accused of planning bombings in Delhi under Chapter IV absconds after being granted bail and fails to appear for multiple hearings; the NIA court declares him a proclaimed offender and orders forfeiture of his bank accounts and land holdings in Punjab.

definitions.definition: A prohibitory order is an order in writing made by the Central Government under sub-section (1) of section 7, prohibiting a person from paying, delivering, transferring or otherwise dealing in any manner whatsoever with any moneys, securities or credits in their custody which are being used or are intended to be used for the purpose of an unlawful association, or with any moneys, securities or credits coming into their custody after the making of the order, except in accordance with the written orders of the Central Government. The term also extends, under sub-section (3) of section 8, to an order prohibiting the use of any article in respect of a notified place.
definitions.plain_english: A prohibitory order is a government directive that freezes a person's ability to use, move, or hand over money, financial assets, or other resources that are believed to be funding a banned organisation. Once this order is served on a person, they cannot do anything with those funds unless the Central Government specifically permits it in writing. A similar order can also ban the use of specific items found in or associated with a notified (government-designated) location.
real_world_examples: The Central Government issues a prohibitory order to a hawala operator in Mumbai after intelligence reveals he is holding funds intended for a banned Kashmiri separatist organisation, preventing him from transferring those funds to any recipient.

A bank manager in Hyderabad who maintains accounts linked to a proscribed organisation receives a prohibitory order, legally barring the bank from allowing any withdrawal, transfer or dealing with the balances in those accounts without Central Government written approval.

A property dealer in Delhi is found to be holding securities on behalf of a designated unlawful association; the Central Government serves a prohibitory order on him, freezing those securities and any further assets that come into his possession.

Following a raid on a suspected terrorist safe house in Chennai declared a notified place under section 8, a prohibitory order is issued in respect of electronic equipment found there, prohibiting any person from using those articles.

A trust in Rajasthan operating as a front for a banned organisation receives a prohibitory order directing its directors not to disburse or transfer any credits held in its accounts, with a gazetted officer simultaneously endorsed to investigate the trust's books.
what_it_covers: An order prohibiting a person from paying, delivering, transferring or dealing in moneys, securities or credits currently in their custody that are linked to an unlawful association.
An order extending the prohibition to any moneys, securities or credits that come into the person's custody after the prohibitory order has been made.
An order made under section 8(3) prohibiting the use of any specific article found at or associated with a notified place declared by the Central Government.

Any written Central Government order served on a corporation, company, bank or association through its officer, director or registered office, restricting financial dealings connected to a banned organisation.
what_it_excludes: General court-ordered injunctions or civil freeze orders not made by the Central Government under section 7 or section 8 of UAPA.
Dealings with moneys, securities or credits that are expressly permitted by a written order of the Central Government, as these fall outside the prohibition.
Orders directed at persons who have no custody or control over any moneys, securities or credits connected to an unlawful association, as the order requires a finding of actual or impending custody.

Criminal sanctions or punishments themselves — the prohibitory order is an administrative directive and does not itself constitute a sentence or fine; penalties arise separately under sections 11 and 12.
Attachment or forfeiture orders issued under separate provisions of the Act, which have a distinct legal character and procedure from a prohibitory order.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an order qualifies as a prohibitory order under section 7(1) or section 8(3) directly determines criminal liability: a person who contravenes a prohibitory order on funds is punishable under section 11 with up to three years imprisonment and an additional fine equal to the value of the assets dealt with, while a person who uses an article in contravention of a prohibitory order relating to a notified place is punishable under section 12 with up to one year imprisonment and fine. Compliance with a valid prohibitory order is therefore a complete defence, whereas non-compliance triggers independent criminal offences under the Act.
