definitions.definition: A promoter, as used in the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, refers to any person who was instrumental in founding, establishing, or incorporating a company, society, or trust and who, at the time an offence under the Act was committed, was in charge of or responsible for the conduct of the business of such company, society, or trust. Such a promoter is deemed guilty of the offence if committed with their consent, connivance, or attributable to their neglect.
definitions.plain_english: A 'promoter' is someone who originally set up or helped create a company, society, or trust. Under UAPA, if that organisation commits a terrorism-related offence, the promoter can be held personally responsible just like a regular director or manager. This means the person who started the organisation cannot escape punishment simply because they are no longer in day-to-day control, if they were involved in or aware of the wrongdoing.
real_world_examples: A founder of a registered NGO in Delhi who set it up and remains on its governing board is found to have channelled funds to a designated terrorist organisation; under UAPA Section 22A, the promoter is personally liable for the offence of terrorist financing.

A co-promoter of a private limited company registered in Mumbai, who originally incorporated it to ostensibly run a media business but allowed the company to be used for spreading anti-national propaganda, can be prosecuted under UAPA along with the company.

The original settler-promoter of a charitable trust in Hyderabad who helped establish it and continued to oversee its finances is found to have knowingly allowed the trust's funds to be routed to a banned unlawful association; they face imprisonment not less than seven years under Section 22C.

A promoter of a firm in Kerala who incorporated the entity and was aware that the firm was being used to recruit members for a terrorist gang, but took no steps to prevent it, is held liable under Section 22A despite claiming ignorance of day-to-day operations.

Two promoters of a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, in Jammu, who facilitated meetings of a terrorist organisation on the society's premises with their consent, are charged jointly with the society under Sections 22B and 22C of UAPA.
what_it_covers: A person who incorporated or founded a company and remains responsible for its business conduct at the time the UAPA offence is committed.
The original settler or founder of a trust or society who was in charge of or responsible for its operations when the unlawful act occurred.
A promoter who did not directly commit the offence but whose consent, connivance, or neglect contributed to the commission of the offence by the company, society, or trust.
A co-promoter of a firm who was jointly responsible for the conduct of the firm's business at the material time.
A promoter who fails to exercise reasonable care to prevent the commission of an offence under UAPA by the entity they established.
what_it_excludes: A person who merely invested in or subscribed to shares of a company without any role in its founding or management, and who is not in charge of the business conduct.
A government-appointed ex officio member representing Central or State Government interests on the governing board, who is expressly excluded under the definition of 'director' in Section 22B.
A promoter who can affirmatively prove that the offence was committed entirely without their knowledge and that they had exercised all reasonable care to prevent its commission.
Employees or staff of the company, society, or trust who had no founding or controlling role and are not responsible for the conduct of the business.
A nominal or dormant promoter who had ceased all association with and responsibility for the entity well before the time the offence was committed.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'promoter' under UAPA determines whether they can be deemed guilty of and prosecuted for terrorism-related offences committed by the company, society, or trust they helped establish, triggering mandatory minimum imprisonment of seven years extendable to life and fines between five crore and ten crore rupees under Section 22C. The definition is critical because it extends criminal liability beyond day-to-day managers to founding members, ensuring that those who create entities used for unlawful activities cannot evade punishment by distancing themselves from operational control.

definitions.definition: 'property' means property and assets of every description whether corporeal or incorporeal, movable or immovable, tangible or intangible and legal documents, deeds and instruments in any form including but not limited to electronic or digital, evidencing title to, or interest in, such property or assets by means of bank credits, travellers' cheques, bank cheques, money orders, shares, securities, bonds, drafts, letters of credit, cash and bank account including fund, however acquired.
definitions.plain_english: Under UAPA, 'property' covers absolutely everything of value that a person or group can own or hold — whether it is something physical like land, cash, or vehicles, or something non-physical like bank account balances, shares, or digital assets. It also includes legal documents that prove ownership or interest in any such asset. The definition is intentionally very broad so that no asset linked to terrorism can escape the law's reach.
real_world_examples: A terrorist organisation in Punjab holds agricultural land registered in the name of a front trust — this immovable land qualifies as 'property' under UAPA and can be attached under Section 25.

A Kashmiri militant operative maintains a savings account with the State Bank of India containing funds transferred from a hawala operator; the bank balance and credits in that account constitute 'property' subject to seizure.

A suspected terrorist cell in Hyderabad holds shares of a private limited company purchased using proceeds of a terrorist financing network; those shares are 'property' and can be forfeited under Section 32.

A handler of a proscribed organisation sends funds via a cryptocurrency wallet to an operative in Delhi; the digital assets and the electronic records evidencing the transaction are treated as 'property' under the Act.

Documents such as a registered sale deed or a title certificate held by a terrorist gang for a safe house in Mumbai are themselves 'property' because they evidence title or interest in an underlying asset.
Travellers' cheques carried by an individual suspected of funding a terrorist organisation across the India-Nepal border are 'property' liable to seizure under UAPA.
what_it_covers: Immovable real estate such as land or buildings owned or controlled by a terrorist organisation or individual terrorist
Bank account balances, credits, fixed deposits, and funds held in any scheduled or cooperative bank in India
Shares, securities, bonds, and debentures whether held in physical certificate form or in a dematerialised DEMAT account
Cash in Indian rupees or any foreign currency physically possessed by a suspect
Electronic or digital assets including cryptocurrency wallets and digital payment records evidencing ownership
Legal instruments such as sale deeds, promissory notes, letters of credit, and money orders that evidence title to or interest in an underlying asset
Incorporeal rights such as intellectual property rights or contractual claims that have economic value
what_it_excludes: Personal labour or services rendered — human effort itself is not 'property' and cannot be attached or forfeited under UAPA
Purely informational or intelligence data that does not evidence title to or interest in an asset (e.g., a raw intelligence report with no economic value)
Contraband items that are inherently illegal and governed exclusively by other statutes such as the NDPS Act or the Arms Act, to the extent those regimes provide a complete code for disposal
Legitimately acquired property of a bona fide transferee who has taken the property for adequate consideration and without knowledge of its terrorist link, who may seek protection under the Act
Sovereign assets of a foreign State or diplomatic property protected under the Vienna Convention, which cannot be attached even if linked to an investigation
definitions.why_it_matters: The scope of 'property' directly determines what assets can be seized, attached, and forfeited under Sections 24, 25, and 32 of UAPA; if an asset qualifies as 'property', investigators and courts have authority to freeze it, attach it pendente lite, and ultimately confiscate it on conviction, whereas assets falling outside this definition cannot be touched under this Act. It also defines the perimeter of the offence of receiving or holding 'proceeds of terrorism' under Section 17 and the prohibition on dealing with funds or property of a listed terrorist organisation under Section 40.

definitions.definition: 'Public functionary' means the constitutional authorities or any other functionary notified in the Official Gazette by the Central Government as public functionary.
definitions.plain_english: A 'public functionary' refers to high-ranking government officials who hold constitutional positions — like the President, Prime Minister, or Chief Ministers — as well as any other official the Central Government specifically designates by publishing their name or category in the Official Gazette. Essentially, it covers important government figures whose death or attempted killing as part of a terrorist act is treated as a terrorist act under UAPA. The Central Government has the power to expand this list by official notification.
real_world_examples: A terrorist plot to assassinate the Prime Minister of India during a public rally in New Delhi would constitute a terrorist act under Section 15, as the Prime Minister is a constitutional authority and thus a public functionary.

An armed attack targeting the Chief Justice of India at the Supreme Court premises would trigger Section 15 liability, since the Chief Justice holds a constitutional office making them a public functionary.

A state governor being targeted for assassination by a militant group in a northeastern state would fall under this provision, as the Governor is a constitutional authority appointed under Article 153 of the Constitution.

If the Central Government issues an Official Gazette notification designating the National Security Advisor as a public functionary, any subsequent attempt on their life by a terrorist group would attract Section 15 of UAPA.

A plot by a terrorist organisation to kill the Chief Minister of a state during a public function would be covered, as the Chief Minister holds a constitutional office under the State Government framework.
what_it_covers: Constitutional authorities such as the President of India, Vice President, Prime Minister, Chief Ministers, Governors, and the Chief Justice of India.
Any other government functionary specifically notified by the Central Government through an Official Gazette notification as a public functionary.
Causing the death of, or attempting to cause the death of, such officials as part of an act intended to threaten the unity, integrity, security, or sovereignty of India.
Senior constitutional office holders of state governments who hold office by virtue of provisions in the Constitution of India.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary government employees or civil servants who do not hold constitutional authority and have not been notified in the Official Gazette as public functionaries.
Members of Parliament or State Legislatures who are not separately notified as public functionaries, as they do not automatically qualify as constitutional authorities under this definition.
Private individuals, corporate executives, or foreign dignitaries who are not constitutional authorities and have not been designated by the Central Government via gazette notification.

definitions.definition: A Public Prosecutor, as used under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, refers to a Public Prosecutor as understood under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, being an officer appointed by the appropriate government to represent the State in criminal proceedings, who is specifically empowered under this Act to be heard on bail applications under Section 43D and to apply to courts for witness protection measures under Section 44.
definitions.plain_english: A Public Prosecutor is a government-appointed lawyer who represents the State in criminal court cases. Under UAPA, this person has special powers — they must be given a chance to speak before any accused terrorist suspect is released on bail, and they can also approach the court to protect the identity of witnesses whose lives may be in danger. Think of them as the government's lawyer in terrorism-related trials.
real_world_examples: In a 2019 NIA case in Delhi involving alleged ISIS module members, the Special Public Prosecutor appeared before the Sessions Court to oppose bail applications of accused persons under UAPA, submitting a detailed report on the progress of investigation to justify detention beyond 90 days up to 180 days.

In a Maoist-related UAPA case in Chhattisgarh, the Public Prosecutor filed an application before the trial court requesting that the identity and address of a key informant-witness be kept secret after receiving credible threats to the witness's life.

In the Bhima Koregaon case in Pune, the Public Prosecutor was given an opportunity of being heard when multiple accused persons sought bail, and the prosecutor placed the case diary before the court to demonstrate prima facie grounds against the accused.

In a 2021 UAPA case in Jammu & Kashmir involving a suspected Lashkar-e-Taiba operative, the Public Prosecutor submitted a progress report to the court explaining why the investigation could not be completed within 90 days, enabling the court to extend custody up to 180 days.

In a Khalistan-related UAPA matter before a Punjab court, the Public Prosecutor moved an application under Section 44 to hold proceedings in camera, citing threats to witnesses, and requested directions preventing publication of witness names in court records.
what_it_covers: A Special Public Prosecutor appointed by the Central Government or State Government specifically for UAPA or NIA cases who must be heard before any accused person is released on bail under Chapters IV and VI of the Act.
A Public Prosecutor who submits a progress report to the court indicating reasons for detention of an accused beyond 90 days, enabling the court to extend custody up to 180 days under Section 43D.
A Public Prosecutor who files an application before a court under Section 44 requesting measures to protect the identity and address of a witness in a UAPA proceeding whose life is in danger.
Any Public Prosecutor appointed under the Code of Criminal Procedure who is assigned to handle UAPA offences before a designated court, including Sessions Court judges or special courts.
what_it_excludes: A private advocate or defence counsel engaged by the accused, even if they are a senior or experienced criminal lawyer, does not qualify as a Public Prosecutor under this Act.
A civil government pleader or standing counsel representing the government in civil or administrative matters does not qualify as a Public Prosecutor for the purposes of UAPA proceedings.

An investigating officer or a police officer conducting the UAPA investigation, even if legally trained, is not a Public Prosecutor and cannot perform the role of being heard on bail or applying for witness protection in that capacity.

An amicus curiae or court-appointed legal aid lawyer, even if assisting the prosecution, does not constitute the Public Prosecutor whose hearing is mandatorily required before bail is granted under Section 43D.
definitions.why_it_matters: The mandatory requirement to hear the Public Prosecutor before granting bail under Section 43D effectively creates a high threshold for bail in UAPA cases — if this opportunity is not given, any bail order may be legally defective and subject to challenge. Additionally, the Public Prosecutor's role under Section 44 directly determines whether witness identities are protected, which in turn affects the integrity of evidence and the safety of witnesses in terrorism trials.

definitions.definition: To 'recruit' means to enlist, persuade, induce, or cause any person or persons to join or participate in the commission of a terrorist act, whether directly or through an intermediary. The term encompasses both the act of recruiting oneself and causing another to carry out such recruitment on one's behalf.
definitions.plain_english: Recruiting means convincing, enrolling, or signing up someone to take part in a terrorist attack or related terrorist activities. This includes not only directly approaching someone but also arranging for others to do the enlisting. Essentially, if you bring someone into a terrorist operation — whether you do it yourself or get someone else to do it — that is 'recruiting' under this law.
real_world_examples: A handler based in Pakistan contacts a youth in Kashmir through social media and persuades him to join a militant group for carrying out a bomb blast in Srinagar — the handler is guilty of recruiting.

A local operative of a banned terrorist organisation visits a madrassa in Hyderabad and convinces students to travel to Syria for waging jihad and committing terrorist acts — this constitutes recruitment under Section 18B.

A member of a Left-Wing Extremist group in Chhattisgarh approaches tribal youth in a village and enrolls them into the Naxal cadre for conducting attacks on security forces and government infrastructure — this is recruitment for a terrorist act.

A financier in Mumbai pays a middleman to visit prisons and identify radicalised inmates who can be brought into an urban terror module after their release to carry out attacks — both the financier and the middleman are liable for recruiting.

An online propagandist running encrypted Telegram channels in India distributes targeted messages to vulnerable individuals urging them to join an ISIS-affiliated cell and carry out lone-wolf attacks on crowded public places — this constitutes recruiting through electronic communication.
what_it_covers: Directly approaching and persuading an individual to participate in a planned terrorist attack.
Using intermediaries or proxies to enlist persons into a terrorist cell or organisation on one's behalf.
Recruiting through digital or electronic means such as social media, encrypted messaging apps, or online propaganda targeting vulnerable individuals in India.
Enrolling persons into a terrorist gang or organisation with the knowledge that they will be used to commit terrorist acts.
Offering monetary compensation, ideological motivation, or coercive inducement to bring persons into a terrorist operation.
what_it_excludes: General employment or hiring of persons for lawful purposes, even if the employer later misuses them, where there is no intent linked to a terrorist act.
Membership in a lawful political, religious, or social organisation that is not designated as a terrorist or unlawful association under UAPA.
Academic research, journalism, or law enforcement activities involving engagement with individuals associated with terrorist groups, where there is no intent to enlist them for a terrorist act.
Persons who are themselves deceived or coerced into joining a group without knowledge that it is engaged in terrorist activity, as they lack the requisite mens rea for the offence of recruitment.
definitions.why_it_matters: If the definition of 'recruit' applies to a person's conduct, that person becomes liable under Section 18B of UAPA for a mandatory minimum sentence of five years up to life imprisonment, along with a fine — a severe non-bailable offence. It directly triggers the application of UAPA's stringent investigation, bail, and prosecution provisions, making the accused subject to extended detention and National Investigation Agency jurisdiction.

definitions.definition: The Review Committee means one or more committees constituted by the Central Government under sub-section (1) of section 37 for the purposes of section 36, each consisting of a Chairperson who is or has been a Judge of a High Court and not more than three other members possessing prescribed qualifications, empowered to review applications challenging the Central Government's rejection of a denotification request to remove an organisation from the Schedule of terrorist organisations.
definitions.plain_english: The Review Committee is a quasi-judicial body set up by the Central Government to provide an independent check on decisions about terrorist organisations. If the government refuses to remove an organisation from its official list of terrorist organisations, anyone affected can ask this committee to review that refusal. The committee, headed by a sitting or retired High Court judge, decides whether the government's rejection was legally sound, similar to how a court would examine such a decision.
real_world_examples: A religious organisation banned and listed as a terrorist organisation under UAPA applies to the Central Government to be de-listed; upon rejection, it approaches the Review Committee within one month, arguing that the grounds for listing no longer exist and that the refusal was legally flawed.

A business owner whose trade association was declared a terrorist organisation petitions the Central Government for de-listing; after rejection, he files a review before the Review Committee constituted by the Central Government, citing denial of natural justice.

An NGO working in conflict-affected areas of Manipur is included in the Schedule as a terrorist organisation; after the Central Government rejects its denotification application, the NGO's representatives appear before the Review Committee chaired by a retired Chief Justice of a High Court to contest the refusal.

A political party's student wing listed as a terrorist organisation in the Schedule challenges the Central Government's refusal to de-list it before the Review Committee, which examines whether the rejection was consistent with judicial review principles such as proportionality and reasonableness.

A person whose livelihood was directly affected by the listing of a local organisation as a terrorist organisation exercises his right as an 'affected person' to seek review before the Review Committee after the Central Government rejects the denotification application.
what_it_covers: Review of the Central Government's rejection of an application to remove an organisation from the Schedule of terrorist organisations under section 35.
Any application made by the terrorist organisation itself or by any person affected by the organisation's inclusion in the Schedule, challenging a refusal of denotification.
Orders directing the Central Government to remove an organisation from the Schedule where the Review Committee finds the rejection to be legally flawed when assessed on judicial review principles.
Oversight of the denotification process to ensure procedural and substantive legality of the Central Government's decision-making regarding listed terrorist organisations.
what_it_excludes: Original decisions to list or notify an organisation as a terrorist organisation under section 35 — the Review Committee only reviews rejections of denotification applications, not the initial listing.

Review of orders relating to individual terrorists, terrorist gangs, or unlawful associations, as the committee's jurisdiction is confined to Schedule-listed terrorist organisations under sections 36 and 37.
General criminal appeals or challenges to prosecutions, convictions, or penalties arising under UAPA — its role is strictly limited to the denotification review process.
Matters relating to forfeiture of property, interception of communications, or other UAPA proceedings unrelated to the Schedule of terrorist organisations.
definitions.why_it_matters: The Review Committee determines whether an organisation remains on the Schedule of terrorist organisations, which directly affects whether the organisation's activities constitute offences under UAPA and whether its members face criminal liability; a committee order in favour of an applicant compels the Central Government to remove the organisation from the Schedule, thereby lifting the statutory disabilities, prohibitions, and criminal exposure associated with membership or support of a listed terrorist organisation.

definitions.definition: Sanction, as used in Section 45 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, refers to the prior written approval granted by the Central Government or, as the case may be, the State Government, without which no court shall take cognizance of an offence under Chapters III, IV, or VI of the Act. Such sanction shall be granted only after an independent review of the evidence gathered during investigation by an authority appointed by the Central Government or State Government, which makes a recommendation within the prescribed time period.
definitions.plain_english: A 'sanction' under UAPA is the official permission that the Central or State Government must give before a court is allowed to even begin hearing a case against someone accused of terrorism-related offences. Before granting this permission, the government must get an independent review of the evidence by a specially appointed authority. Without this permission, the court simply cannot start the legal process, no matter how strong the evidence may be.
real_world_examples: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) completes its investigation against an accused alleged to have funded a banned terrorist organisation under Chapter VI of UAPA; before the NIA court takes cognizance of the chargesheet, the Central Government must review the independent authority's recommendation and formally grant sanction for prosecution.

A state police force arrests individuals in Punjab for alleged conspiracy to wage war through unlawful means under Chapter III of UAPA; the state cannot independently grant sanction — only the Central Government can authorise prosecution, and it must do so based on an independent review of the evidence gathered during the investigation.

The Delhi Police files a chargesheet against members of an alleged urban Naxal network under Chapter IV of UAPA; the Delhi Government (as State Government) must obtain the independent review report and then grant prosecution sanction before the Sessions Court can take cognizance of the offences.

A suspected member of a designated terrorist organisation is arrested in Maharashtra for financing terror activities; the Maharashtra Government seeks the independent authority's report before granting sanction for prosecution under Chapter IV, and the Central Government must separately grant sanction for charges relating to offences against a foreign country's government.

In a case involving alleged support to a foreign terrorist organisation committing acts against the government of Afghanistan, the Central Government's sanction is mandatory — even if state police conducted the investigation — because the offence is committed against a foreign country's government as specified in Section 45(1).

A special NIA court in Hyderabad receives a chargesheet in a Maoist-related bombing case; the court clerk flags that Central Government sanction under Section 45 has not been filed along with the chargesheet, and the judge cannot proceed to take cognizance until the sanction document is produced on record.
what_it_covers: Written prior approval by the Central Government permitting prosecution of offences under Chapter III of UAPA (unlawful activities related offences).
Prior approval by the Central Government or State Government (as applicable) for prosecution of offences under Chapters IV and VI of UAPA (terrorist activities and terrorist organisations).
Sanction granted specifically by the Central Government for offences under Chapters IV and VI committed against the government of a foreign country.
The process of independent review by an authority appointed by the Central or State Government that must precede and inform the grant of sanction.
Time-bound sanction orders issued within the period prescribed under rules framed under Section 52 of the Act.
what_it_excludes: Sanction for prosecution of offences under laws other than UAPA, such as IPC or Arms Act charges filed in the same case — courts may take cognizance of those charges independently.

Administrative approvals or executive orders issued by the government for purposes other than prosecution, such as notification of an unlawful association or attachment of property, which are not 'sanctions' under Section 45.

Sanction granted by police officers, investigating officers, or Public Prosecutors — only the Central Government or State Government (or their authorised officers) can grant valid sanction under Section 45.

Post-cognizance approvals or retrospective sanctions — sanction must be obtained before the court takes cognizance; a court cannot cure the absence of sanction by accepting it after proceedings have commenced.

Review or recommendation by the independent authority itself — this is a prerequisite to sanction, not the sanction itself; the recommendation is not binding on the government but the government cannot bypass the review process.

definitions.definition: 'Schedule' means the Schedule to this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The 'Schedule' refers to the official list or appendix attached at the end of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act itself. This Schedule contains the names of organisations that have been designated as terrorist organisations by the Indian government. Any organisation listed there is automatically treated as a terrorist organisation under the law.
real_world_examples: When the Indian government banned Jaish-e-Mohammed, it was added to the Schedule of UAPA, making it a 'terrorist organisation' and triggering all legal consequences under the Act against its members and supporters.

When a court examines whether a person accused under Section 38 (membership of a terrorist organisation) is guilty, it checks whether the organisation in question appears in the Schedule to confirm it qualifies as a terrorist organisation.

Under Section 36, when the Central Government adds a new organisation such as the Islamic State (ISIS/ISIL) to the Schedule, all subsequent activities related to that organisation—financing, recruitment, or support—become punishable offences under UAPA.

If an organisation operates under an alias or a name identical to one listed in the Schedule, it is also treated as a terrorist organisation even without a fresh notification, illustrating the Schedule's binding legal effect.

When a designated authority reviews whether to continue the ban on a listed organisation like the Students Islamic Movement of India (SIMI), the process involves amending or retaining entries in the Schedule, which directly determines the legality of the organisation's activities across India.
what_it_covers: All organisations formally listed as terrorist organisations in the appendix attached to the UAPA, such as Lashkar-e-Taiba, Jaish-e-Mohammed, and others notified by the Central Government.
Any organisation operating under the same name as one listed in the Schedule, which is automatically deemed a terrorist organisation without requiring a separate listing.
The operative legal reference that courts use under Sections 36 and 38 to determine whether an entity qualifies as a 'terrorist organisation' for the purposes of prosecution and adjudication.
what_it_excludes: Organisations declared as 'unlawful associations' under the UAPA that are not specifically listed in the Schedule as terrorist organisations—these are governed by separate provisions.
Terrorist gangs as defined under Section 2, which are informal associations involved in terrorist acts but are not formal organisations capable of being listed in the Schedule.

Foreign or international terrorist organisations that may be banned in other jurisdictions but have not been formally added to the Schedule of the UAPA by the Indian government, and therefore do not attract the legal consequences under Sections 36 and 38 by virtue of that foreign listing alone.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an organisation appears in the Schedule is the critical threshold that determines whether a person can be prosecuted under Section 38 for membership of a terrorist organisation or under Section 36 for related offences; without a Schedule listing, the specific offences tied to 'terrorist organisations' cannot be invoked, and the associated stringent penalties and bail restrictions under UAPA would not apply.

definitions.definition: 'Secession of a part of the territory of India from the Union' includes the assertion of any claim to determine whether such part will remain a part of the territory of India.
definitions.plain_english: Secession means the act of breaking away or attempting to break away a part of India from the rest of the country. Under this law, even asserting or claiming the right to decide whether a region should remain part of India is treated as secession. It does not require actual separation — even the demand or assertion of such a right is enough to fall within this definition.
real_world_examples: A separatist organisation in Jammu & Kashmir publicly demanding that the region should hold an independence referendum to decide whether it wants to remain part of India would fall under this definition of secession.

A group in Manipur circulating pamphlets or posting on social media asserting that the state has the right to determine its own status and should separate from the Indian Union would constitute secession under UAPA.

Leaders of an underground movement in Nagaland issuing manifestos claiming sovereign independence for the Naga people and asserting that Nagaland is not lawfully part of India would be engaging in secessionist activity.
An organisation based in Punjab promoting the Khalistan movement and asserting claims that the Punjab region should be carved out of India as a separate nation would be covered under this definition.

A foreign-funded group in Tamil Nadu advocating for a separate Tamil Eelam state by asserting that the Tamil-speaking parts of India should determine their own political future outside the Indian Union would trigger this definition.
what_it_covers: Any public assertion or claim that a particular region of India has the right to determine whether it will remain part of India, even without actual violence or physical separation.
Propaganda, pamphlets, speeches, or online content that demand an independence vote or referendum for any part of Indian territory.
Organised movements that assert the legal or political right of a region to secede, regardless of whether the demand is accompanied by violence.
Actions by individuals or associations that support, incite, or encourage others to make or act upon claims of secession from the Indian Union.
Any formal declaration or manifesto by a group claiming that a part of India is not legitimately part of the Union and should be separated.
what_it_excludes: Academic or scholarly discussion of secession as a theoretical concept in international law or political science, where no actual claim or incitement is being made.
Legitimate political advocacy for greater autonomy, federalism, or constitutional reorganisation of states within the framework of the Indian Union, without asserting the right to separate.
Journalistic reporting or documentary coverage of secessionist movements elsewhere in the world or even within India, provided it does not assert or support any claim to secede.
Cession of territory, which is a distinct concept defined separately in the Act as involving transfer or admission of foreign claims over Indian territory, not internal separation.

Statements made by foreign governments or international bodies about Indian territory that are countered by diplomatic means, as this definition applies to individuals and associations acting under UAPA.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as 'secession' under UAPA directly determines whether that act constitutes 'unlawful activity' under Section 2, which in turn determines whether an individual or association can be declared an unlawful association under Section 3 and its members prosecuted for offences carrying heavy penalties including imprisonment. It also triggers the power to ban organisations, attach property, and invoke special court jurisdiction under the Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'securities' is not separately defined in the Act but is used as a component of 'property' under Section 2, where property is defined to include 'shares, securities, bonds, drafts, letters of credit' among other financial instruments; and is used in Section 7 in conjunction with 'moneys' and 'credits' to refer to financial instruments of value held in custody that may be used or intended to be used for the purposes of an unlawful association.
definitions.plain_english: Securities in this law refers to financial instruments like shares, bonds, government securities, debentures, or similar documents that represent financial value or ownership rights. These are instruments that can hold or transfer monetary value and may be used to fund unlawful or terrorist activities. Under UAPA, if such instruments are connected to an unlawful association or terrorist activity, the government can restrict or prohibit dealings in them.
real_world_examples: A banned organisation in India holds government treasury bonds worth ₹50 lakh in the name of a sympathiser; the Central Government can prohibit that person from transferring or encashing those bonds under Section 7.
A terrorist organisation channels funds through purchase of listed company shares on the Bombay Stock Exchange; those shares qualify as 'securities' and can be frozen or seized under UAPA provisions.

A person suspected of financing a terrorist gang is found to hold corporate debentures issued by an Indian company on behalf of the gang; these debentures constitute 'securities' and dealings in them can be prohibited.

An unlawful association declared under Section 3 of UAPA receives National Savings Certificates purchased by sympathisers; these government-backed securities fall within the scope of 'securities' under the Act, triggering prohibitory action.

Hawala operators funding a terrorist organisation convert cash into mutual fund units and bonds; the bond holdings are treated as 'securities' forming part of 'proceeds of terrorism', enabling attachment under UAPA.
what_it_covers: Government securities such as treasury bonds, National Savings Certificates, and sovereign bonds held on behalf of or for the benefit of an unlawful association or terrorist organisation.

Corporate financial instruments including shares, debentures, bonds, and convertible instruments listed or unlisted in Indian markets, where they are used or intended to be used for terrorist or unlawful purposes.
Debt instruments such as promissory notes, certificates of deposit, and fixed deposits documented as securities that are traceable to funds derived from or intended for terrorist activity.
Mutual fund units, exchange-traded fund certificates, and similar investment instruments when held as part of proceeds of terrorism or for financing an unlawful association.
Foreign securities or instruments held in India or by persons in India on behalf of a banned organisation or individual terrorist.
what_it_excludes: Physical cash or currency notes, which are separately categorised as 'cash' or 'moneys' rather than securities under the Act.
Immovable property such as land or buildings, which fall under the broader definition of 'property' but are not securities.
Personal letters of credit or bank drafts that are not in the nature of tradeable or investment instruments, though these are listed separately in the definition of 'property'.
Intellectual property rights, trademarks, or patents, which may be incorporeal property but do not constitute 'securities' in the financial instrument sense.
Oral or informal credit arrangements and unrecorded hawala transactions that have not been reduced to any written instrument or document evidencing value.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an asset qualifies as 'securities' under UAPA determines whether the Central Government can invoke Section 7 to issue a prohibitory order restraining a person from transferring, delivering, or dealing in those instruments when they are connected to an unlawful association, thereby freezing financial resources of banned organisations. It also determines whether such instruments are treated as 'proceeds of terrorism' or 'property' under Section 2, which triggers liability for attachment, forfeiture, and criminal prosecution under the Act.

definitions.definition: The term 'security' is not formally defined in Section 2 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967; however, as used in Section 7, 'securities' refers to financial instruments including shares, bonds, debentures, and other negotiable or transferable instruments representing financial value or ownership interest, which are in the custody of any person and are being used or intended to be used for the purposes of an unlawful association.
definitions.plain_english: In simple terms, 'securities' under UAPA refers to financial instruments like shares, bonds, government securities, or debentures that someone holds or controls. If these financial instruments are being used or are planned to be used to fund or support a banned (unlawful) organisation, the government can step in and stop the person from dealing with them. Essentially, it covers paper or digital proof of financial value that could be misused to support terrorist or unlawful groups.
real_world_examples: A Mumbai-based broker holds government bonds (G-secs) belonging to an individual whose association has been declared unlawful under Section 3 of UAPA; the Central Government can prohibit the broker from transferring or redeeming those bonds.

A member of a banned organisation in Punjab maintains demat account holdings of NSE-listed company shares that are intended to fund the organisation's operations; the Central Government can issue a prohibitory order freezing those share transactions.

A Kashmiri separatist group funnels funds through corporate debentures held by a sympathiser in Delhi; the Central Government, upon inquiry, can bar the debenture holder from transferring or dealing in those instruments.

A trust based in Hyderabad holds mutual fund units and fixed-income securities on behalf of an association subsequently declared unlawful; under Section 7, the Central Government can prohibit the trustee from liquidating or transferring those securities.

A financier in Chennai possesses RBI Treasury Bills acquired using proceeds linked to a banned outfit; the Central Government can issue a written order preventing him from encashing or transferring those instruments.
what_it_covers: Government bonds, treasury bills, and G-secs held by a person on behalf of or for use by an unlawful association.
Listed company shares or debentures held in physical or demat form that are being used or intended to be used for the purposes of a banned organisation.
Mutual fund units, corporate bonds, and other transferable financial instruments in the custody of any individual or entity linked to an unlawful association.
Promissory notes, bills of exchange, and other negotiable instruments that represent financial value and are traceable to or intended for use by an unlawful association.
what_it_excludes: Physical cash or liquid money held by a person, which is separately addressed under 'moneys' in Section 7 and is not classified as a security.
Immovable property such as land or buildings, which falls under the definition of 'property' in Section 2 rather than 'securities' as used in Section 7.
Credits or bank account balances, which are separately enumerated alongside 'moneys' and 'securities' in Section 7 and thus constitute a distinct category.
Personal jewellery, gold, or other physical commodities not representing a financial instrument or ownership interest in any legal or corporate entity.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an instrument qualifies as a 'security' under Section 7 determines whether the Central Government can issue a written prohibitory order preventing the holder from paying, delivering, transferring, or otherwise dealing with it, thereby cutting off a critical financial lifeline to a declared unlawful association. Failure to comply with such a prohibitory order can expose the custodian to criminal liability under UAPA, making the correct identification of 'securities' essential for both enforcement agencies and financial intermediaries.

definitions.definition: Seizure means the act by which an investigating officer, with the prior written approval of the Director General of Police of the State, takes physical custody and control of any property that is believed to represent proceeds of terrorism, or detains any cash suspected to be intended for use in terrorism or forming part of the resources of a terrorist organisation, pending production before and confirmation by the Designated Authority.
definitions.plain_english: Seizure is when a police investigating officer physically takes possession of property or cash suspected to be connected to terrorism, preventing the owner from using or moving it. The officer needs written permission from the state's top police official before seizing the property. Once seized, the property must be brought before a Designated Authority within 48 hours, who then decides whether to keep the seizure in place or release the property.
real_world_examples: An NIA officer investigating a Maoist financing network in Chhattisgarh, with written approval from the DGP, seizes a fleet of vehicles and land parcels registered in the name of a suspected front company, as the properties are believed to represent proceeds of terrorism.

During a crackdown on a Lashkar-e-Taiba funding channel in Jammu & Kashmir, an investigating officer seizes a large amount of foreign currency cash found at a hawala operator's premises, suspecting it is intended to fund a planned terrorist attack.

In Mumbai, an officer investigating a terror financing case seizes bank-issued bearer cheques and traveller's cheques worth crores found at the residence of a suspect believed to be channelling funds to a proscribed organisation.

Following a tip-off in Hyderabad, an Anti-Terrorism Squad officer with DGP approval seizes gold bars and high-value credit cards held by a suspect, on reasonable grounds that these form part of the economic resources of a banned terrorist outfit.

An investigating officer in Delhi seizes a commercial property registered in the name of a shell company, after gathering evidence that rental income from it was being systematically funnelled to a terrorist gang operating in the Northeast.
what_it_covers: Movable property such as cash, vehicles, jewellery, or electronic equipment believed to represent proceeds of terrorism seized with DGP's prior written approval.

Cash in the form of coins, currency notes, postal orders, traveller's cheques, credit/debit cards, or banker's drafts suspected to be intended for use in terrorism or forming part of a terrorist organisation's resources.
Property seized during investigation of offences under Chapter IV (punishment of terrorist acts) or Chapter VI (terrorist organisations) of UAPA.
Property that is subsequently produced before the Designated Authority for confirmation or revocation of the seizure order within sixty days.
Forfeited property whose day of seizure is used as the reference date for calculating reasonable interest in case of acquittal or modification of forfeiture order under Section 28.
what_it_excludes: Immovable property that cannot be physically seized and is instead dealt with by an attachment order directing non-transfer without prior permission, rather than seizure.
Property belonging to bona fide third-party claimants who successfully establish before the Designated Authority under Section 30 that their property is not liable to seizure or attachment.
Property or assets seized under other laws (such as PMLA or the Customs Act) in unrelated proceedings not connected to an offence under Chapter IV or Chapter VI of UAPA.
Cash retained beyond 48 hours without a Designated Authority order — such retention without authority is implicitly excluded from valid seizure.
Actions taken without prior written approval of the DGP of the concerned State, which would not constitute a lawful seizure under the Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The moment a valid seizure is made, the owner loses the right to deal with or transfer the property, and the clock starts for mandatory production before the Designated Authority within 48 hours; failure to follow seizure procedures can invalidate the entire chain of forfeiture proceedings under Sections 25–28, while a valid seizure is the prerequisite for any subsequent forfeiture order and determines the date from which interest is calculated under Section 28 if the property must be returned.

definitions.definition: A 'settlor' means a person who creates or establishes a trust by transferring property or assets into it, and who, at the time an offence under this Act is committed, may be deemed personally liable if they were in charge of or responsible for the conduct of the business of the trust. The term is used in the context of offences committed by trusts, treating the settlor on par with a promoter of a company or society for the purposes of criminal liability under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: A settlor is the person who originally sets up a trust by putting their money, property, or other assets into it. Under UAPA, if a trust commits a terrorist-related offence, the settlor can be held personally responsible — just like the head of a company would be — if they were in control of or responsible for how the trust was run. This means the person who created the trust cannot escape punishment simply because the trust itself is a separate legal body.
real_world_examples: A wealthy businessman in Mumbai creates a charitable trust, transfers crores of rupees into it, and remains its controlling authority; if the trust is found to be financing terrorist organisations, he as the settlor can be prosecuted under UAPA alongside the trust itself.

A religious leader in Hyderabad establishes a trust for educational purposes, acts as its day-to-day manager, and the trust is later found to be channelling funds to a notified unlawful association; the leader, as settlor, is liable to imprisonment of not less than seven years under Section 22C.

A family in Delhi registers a private trust under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, and the settlor — the patriarch who created it — is found to have knowingly allowed the trust's funds to be used for procuring explosives for a terrorist gang; he faces prosecution and a fine of up to ten crore rupees.

An NRI individual settles a trust in Chennai, appoints trustees, but retains effective control over financial decisions; when the trust is found to have made transfers to a proscribed terrorist organisation abroad, the NRI settlor is treated as personally liable under Section 22C of UAPA.

A social organisation in Jammu creates a trust and its settlor continues to supervise its activities; upon discovery that the trust was used to recruit individuals for terrorist training, the settlor is held equally guilty alongside the trustees under Sections 22B and 22C.
what_it_covers: A person who creates and registers a trust under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 and retains control or responsibility over its operations at the time of the offence.
A settlor who is actively involved in the day-to-day management or financial decisions of the trust when the trust commits an offence under UAPA.
A settlor who, though not a formal trustee, exercises de facto control or oversight over the trust's conduct of business at the relevant time.
A settlor who is proven to have consented to, connived in, or been negligent about the trust's involvement in terrorist activity or financing.
what_it_excludes: A settlor who has completely relinquished all control and responsibility over the trust before the time the offence was committed, and who can demonstrate no involvement in trust management.
A beneficiary of the trust who did not create it and holds no managerial or supervisory role in its operations.

A trustee or office-bearer appointed by the settlor who independently manages the trust without the settlor's knowledge or direction — such persons are governed separately under the 'trustee' or 'director' definitions.
A person who merely contributed funds to a trust as a donor but did not create or settle it and has no control over its conduct.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a person qualifies as a 'settlor' under UAPA directly determines whether they can be held criminally liable for offences committed by the trust, including terrorism financing and support of unlawful associations, attracting mandatory imprisonment of not less than seven years up to life and fines between five crore and ten crore rupees under Section 22C. The classification also determines who must be proceeded against alongside the trust entity, ensuring that those who created and controlled the trust cannot shield themselves behind its separate legal identity.

definitions.definition: 'Society' means any body corporate registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (21 of 1860) or any other State Act governing the registration of societies.
definitions.plain_english: A 'society' under UAPA refers to any formally registered organisation or group that has been incorporated under the central Societies Registration Act of 1860 or an equivalent registration law of any Indian state. These are typically non-profit or charitable bodies that have obtained legal recognition by registering with the appropriate government authority. Once registered, the society is treated as a legal entity that can be held accountable under UAPA if it commits or facilitates a terrorist offence.
real_world_examples: A registered cultural society in Maharashtra that is found to be channelling funds to a banned terrorist organisation and whose managing committee members are prosecuted under UAPA Section 22B for enabling terrorist financing.

An educational society registered under the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Public Societies Registration Act that is discovered to have provided logistical support to a terrorist gang operating in the region, leading to criminal liability for its promoters and office-bearers.

A charitable society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 in Delhi that is used as a front organisation to recruit members for a terrorist organisation, resulting in prosecution of its secretary and director under Section 22C for the recruitment offence.

A welfare society registered in Jammu & Kashmir under the relevant state societies registration law whose governing board members are found to have consented to the society's premises being used for planning a terrorist act, making them personally liable under UAPA.

A religious society registered in Tamil Nadu that collects donations ostensibly for social welfare but diverts proceeds to fund a terrorist organisation abroad, with the Enforcement Directorate proceeding against both the society and its office-bearers under UAPA's provisions on proceeds of terrorism.
what_it_covers: Any society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (central legislation), such as literary, scientific, or charitable associations that have obtained a certificate of registration.

Any body corporate registered under a State Act governing registration of societies, such as the Karnataka Societies Registration Act or the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act where societies are covered, that has committed or facilitated a UAPA offence.

The promoters, directors, managers, secretaries, and other officers of the registered society who were in charge of and responsible for the conduct of its business at the time the UAPA offence was committed.
A society that has acted with the consent or connivance of its governing board members in committing a UAPA offence, thereby attracting both institutional and individual criminal liability.
what_it_excludes: Unregistered or informal groups, associations, or collectives that have not obtained legal registration under any central or state societies registration law, even if they function like a society in practice.
Companies incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, which are separately defined and governed under Section 22A of UAPA and not covered by the definition of 'society'.
Trusts registered under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 or state trust registration laws, which are separately defined and treated as a distinct legal category under Section 22B.

Government bodies, statutory corporations, or entities established directly by an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature, which are not registered under societies registration laws and fall outside this definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'society' under UAPA determines whether its promoters, directors, managers, and other officers can be held vicariously and personally liable for UAPA offences committed by the entity, including being sentenced to a minimum of seven years' imprisonment and fined between five and ten crore rupees under Section 22C. Without this classification, individual officers of the registered body may escape criminal accountability for terrorist acts committed through or by the organisation.

definitions.definition: Sovereignty, as used in this Act, refers to the supreme and independent authority of India as a nation-state, including its power to govern itself without external interference; any act intended to threaten, disrupt, disclaim, or undermine this supreme authority constitutes an unlawful activity or terrorist act under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: Sovereignty means India's right and power to govern itself as an independent country, free from control by any foreign power or internal group seeking to undermine its authority. Under UAPA, any action — whether by words, deeds, or violence — that threatens India's status as a self-governing nation is treated as a serious offence. This includes acts of terrorism that aim to weaken the Indian government's ability to function or assert its authority.
real_world_examples: A terrorist organisation based in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir launches armed attacks on Indian Army posts in Jammu with the stated aim of forcing India to cede the region — this directly threatens India's sovereignty and constitutes a terrorist act under Section 15.

A group publishes and distributes manifestos in multiple Indian cities declaring that certain northeastern states are not legally part of India and calling for armed rebellion against Indian administrative authority, thereby disclaiming India's sovereign control over those territories.

A foreign-funded organisation operating in India conducts a sustained campaign urging the United Nations to recognise a secessionist region as an independent state, actively undermining India's sovereign claim over that territory.

Cybercriminals backed by a hostile foreign state launch coordinated attacks on India's defence communication networks and election infrastructure, intending to paralyse the government's capacity to function, thereby threatening India's sovereign functioning.

An individual aligned with a banned terrorist organisation plants explosives at Parliament House with the stated intent of destabilising the Indian government and forcing a change in India's constitutional order — a direct threat to national sovereignty.
what_it_covers: Acts of violence or intimidation intended to force India to surrender governance or control over any part of its territory to a foreign state or non-state actor.
Propaganda, publications, or spoken words that disclaim, question, or disrupt India's supreme authority to govern itself as an independent nation.
Cyberattacks, bombings, or other acts of force aimed at disabling or undermining the functioning of India's government, military, or constitutional institutions.
Foreign-funded campaigns or organisations operating within India that seek to delegitimise India's authority over its recognised territory.
Armed insurgencies or militant operations aimed at replacing Indian governance with a parallel authority in any region of India.
what_it_excludes: Legitimate political dissent, democratic protest, or peaceful advocacy for constitutional amendments or policy changes, which do not disclaim or threaten India's sovereign authority.
Academic or journalistic commentary critiquing government policies or actions, provided it does not actively seek to undermine or disrupt India's sovereignty.
Diplomatic negotiations or legal proceedings before international tribunals where India itself is a party and voluntarily participates in resolving territorial disputes.
Acts by foreign governments exercising their own sovereign functions within their own territories, even if those acts are diplomatically adverse to India.
Statements by recognised political parties within India advocating for greater autonomy or federalism within the constitutional framework, without seeking to break away from the Union.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act threatens India's sovereignty is a key determinant under Section 15 for classifying it as a 'terrorist act,' which triggers stringent consequences including enhanced punishment, extended pre-trial detention, and investigation by the National Investigation Agency; failure to satisfy this element may mean the act is prosecuted under ordinary criminal law rather than the harsher UAPA framework.

definitions.definition: 'State Government', in relation to a Union territory, means the Administrator thereof.
definitions.plain_english: In most cases, 'State Government' refers to the elected government of a particular Indian state, such as Maharashtra or Tamil Nadu. However, for Union Territories (like Lakshadweep or Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu), which do not have fully elected state governments, 'State Government' means the Administrator appointed by the Central Government to govern that territory. This distinction ensures the law applies uniformly across all parts of India, whether they are states or Union Territories.
real_world_examples: When the Government of Maharashtra issues a notification under Section 34 of UAPA designating an officer as the Designated Authority for terrorist-related investigations, it acts in its capacity as the 'State Government' under the Act.

In the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir, the Lieutenant Governor (acting as Administrator) exercises powers vested in the 'State Government' under Sections 34 and 45 of UAPA, such as sanctioning prosecutions or issuing relevant orders.

The Government of Punjab, dealing with a cross-border terror module operating within its territory, exercises 'State Government' powers under UAPA to coordinate with central agencies and take action under Section 45 for sanction of prosecution.

In Puducherry, a Union Territory with a legislature, the Administrator (Lieutenant Governor) still functions as the 'State Government' for the purposes of UAPA when exercising powers under Sections 34 and 45, including granting or refusing sanction for prosecution of accused persons.

The Telangana State Government, upon receiving a request from the National Investigation Agency, acts as 'State Government' under UAPA to appoint a Designated Authority not below the rank of Secretary for overseeing terror-financing cases within the state.

In Andaman and Nicobar Islands, where there is no elected state legislature, the Administrator exercises all 'State Government' functions under UAPA, including sanctioning prosecution of individuals suspected of unlawful activities under Section 45.
what_it_covers: The elected government of any Indian state (e.g., Government of Kerala, Government of Uttar Pradesh) exercising powers under UAPA within its territorial jurisdiction.

The Administrator of a Union Territory (e.g., Lieutenant Governor of Delhi or Puducherry) when exercising UAPA powers such as designating authorities or sanctioning prosecutions within that Union Territory.
The Administrator of a Union Territory without a legislature (e.g., Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar Islands) who fully substitutes as the 'State Government' for all purposes under the Act.
State-level authorities empowered to issue notifications, appoint Designated Authorities not below Secretary rank, and grant or refuse sanctions for prosecution under Sections 34 and 45 of UAPA.
what_it_excludes: The Central Government, which is a separately defined and distinct authority under UAPA with its own set of powers and obligations, including appointing Central Designated Authorities at Joint Secretary level.
Local bodies such as Municipal Corporations, Panchayats, or District Administrations, which are not the 'State Government' and cannot exercise powers reserved for it under UAPA.
State police officers or individual state officials acting in their personal or departmental capacity, as they do not constitute the 'State Government' itself for purposes of this Act.
High Courts or State Tribunals, which are judicial bodies and not part of the executive 'State Government' for the purposes of the definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identity of the 'State Government' is critical under UAPA because Sections 34 and 45 vest specific powers — including the appointment of Designated Authorities and the grant of sanction for prosecution — exclusively in the State Government; if the wrong authority exercises these powers, any resulting notification, designation, or prosecution sanction may be legally invalid. Correctly identifying the 'State Government' also determines whether a Union Territory Administrator or an elected state cabinet holds decision-making authority, which directly affects the chain of accountability in terrorism-related proceedings.

definitions.definition: A 'summary case' under Section 43F of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act means a case tried summarily under Chapter XXI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, where the procedure prescribed therein (except sub-section (2) of section 262 of the Code) applies to an offence of failure to furnish information or deliberately furnishing false information under sub-section (2) of Section 43F.
definitions.plain_english: A summary case is a fast-track type of criminal trial used for relatively minor offences where the full lengthy trial procedure is not required. In the context of UAPA, when someone refuses to give information requested by an investigating officer, or gives false information, the resulting criminal case is tried quickly using a simplified court procedure. This means the court can decide the matter faster without going through all the elaborate steps of a regular trial.
real_world_examples: An investigating officer in Mumbai, probing a terrorist financing case under UAPA, formally requests a private bank to furnish transaction records of a suspected terrorist. The bank manager refuses without any valid reason. The prosecution of the bank manager for this refusal is conducted as a summary case before a Magistrate, with an expedited hearing and simplified procedure.

A telecommunications company in Delhi is asked to provide call records related to a UAPA offence investigation. The company's compliance officer deliberately submits fabricated or incomplete records. The subsequent criminal proceeding against the officer is tried as a summary case under Chapter XXI of the CrPC.

During a National Investigation Agency (NIA) probe into a Maoist-linked terrorist activity in Chhattisgarh, a local government authority is required to furnish land records. The authority fails to comply within the stipulated time. The trial for non-compliance is conducted summarily, allowing the Magistrate to dispose of the matter quickly.

A Hawala operator in Hyderabad is asked by a Superintendent of Police-approved investigating officer to provide financial ledgers relevant to a terrorist funding probe. The operator furnishes deliberately false accounts. The case against the operator is tried as a summary case, with the simplified CrPC Chapter XXI procedure applied, enabling faster adjudication.

An NGO official in Srinagar, whose organisation is under UAPA scrutiny, is asked to provide membership and funding records. The official stonewalls the investigation by refusing to hand over documents. The prosecution for this failure is treated as a summary case, ensuring speedy disposal without prolonged trial proceedings.
what_it_covers: Prosecution of any person who fails to furnish information required under Section 43F(1) of UAPA, tried using the simplified summary procedure of CrPC Chapter XXI.
Prosecution of any person or entity that deliberately furnishes false information in response to a request made under Section 43F(1), conducted as a summary trial.
Application of all provisions of CrPC Chapter XXI (except section 262(2)) to the trial of offences under Section 43F(2), including reduced procedural formalities and quicker disposal.

The law treats terrorism as a broad concept that includes planning, financing, supporting, and actually carrying out such acts.

A radical organisation recruits youth through online platforms in Hyderabad, trains them in bomb-making, and plans suicide attacks on government buildings to coerce policy change — every stage of this operation falls within terrorism.

A terrorist network operating in Punjab raises funds through hawala channels and uses the money to procure weapons for attacking political leaders and spreading communal violence, thereby threatening the sovereignty and unity of India — this entire operation constitutes terrorism.

Members of a banned organisation in Tamil Nadu organise camps in remote forests to train operatives in guerrilla warfare techniques aimed at overthrowing state authority through violent insurrection — this is terrorism under the Act.

An individual spreads biological agents in a crowded Delhi market to cause mass casualties and instil fear in the civilian population — such use of weapons capable of mass destruction falls squarely within terrorism.

Cyberattacks or attacks on critical infrastructure carried out with intent to threaten national security or strike terror in the populace.

definitions.plain_english: A terrorist is someone who carries out, attempts, or is involved in an act of terrorism as defined under the UAPA. A member of a proscribed organisation who recruits and trains youth in a camp along the Indo-Bangladesh border for committing violent acts against Indian citizens is considered a terrorist under the Act.

A person in Chennai who procures and supplies explosives to a network planning simultaneous attacks on government buildings to coerce the Union Government is liable to be designated a terrorist under UAPA.
An individual who hijacks a passenger aircraft in Indian airspace and threatens to crash it unless political demands are met is acting as a terrorist within the meaning of the Act.

definitions.plain_english: A 'terrorist act' is any action carried out with the intention of threatening India's unity, integrity, security, or sovereignty, or to spread terror among people in India or abroad, using explosives, firearms, or other dangerous means. definitions.definition: 'Terrorist activity' as used in the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act encompasses any action taken to further the activity of a terrorist organisation, including inviting support for such organisation, arranging or managing meetings to support or further its activity, or addressing meetings to encourage support for or further the activity of a terrorist organisation, as governed under Section 39.
definitions.plain_english: Terrorist activity refers to any action that helps or promotes the work of a terrorist organisation. This includes calling for people to support such groups, organising or running meetings in their favour, or giving speeches to encourage others to back them. Even if money is not involved, simply promoting or facilitating the group's goals counts as terrorist activity under this law.
real_world_examples: A person in Kashmir organises a secret gathering where attendees are encouraged to provide recruits and moral support to a designated terrorist organisation like Lashkar-e-Taiba, thereby facilitating its continued operations.

An individual in Delhi publicly delivers a speech at a community hall urging the audience to show solidarity with and support the ideology and goals of a banned terrorist outfit such as the Indian Mujahideen.

A person in Punjab arranges and manages a video conference meeting knowing that a self-professed member of Khalistan Liberation Force will address it to rally support for the organisation's activities.

An activist in Chennai invites others via encrypted messaging apps to join and back a designated terrorist organisation's cause, even without soliciting direct financial contributions, thereby furthering its activity.

A student union leader in Hyderabad organises a seminar that he knows will be addressed by a person who publicly professes association with a proscribed terrorist group, intending to further the group's recruitment drive.

Delivering a speech or address at a meeting for the purpose of encouraging support for a terrorist organisation or advancing its activities.

what_it_excludes: Provision of money or other property to a terrorist organisation, which falls under Section 40 and constitutes a separate and distinct offence rather than mere 'terrorist activity' under Section 39.

definitions.definition: Terrorist fund means any property or funds that are used, intended to be used, or allocated for the purpose of financing or facilitating terrorist acts, terrorist organisations, or terrorist activities. Though not formally defined in a standalone provision, as used in Section 21 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, it refers to the pool of resources through which terrorism is resourced, sustained, or advanced, and from which property may be acquired.
definitions.plain_english: A terrorist fund is essentially a pool of money or assets that is collected, held, or used to support terrorism in any way — including planning attacks, buying weapons, paying operatives, or running terrorist organisations. If someone knowingly owns property that was bought using such funds, they are committing a serious crime under Indian law. It does not matter whether the person carried out any attack themselves — simply holding property linked to such funds is enough to attract punishment.
real_world_examples: A hawala operator in Mumbai channels money received from a Pakistan-based terrorist outfit to sleeper cells in India; the funds transferred through this informal network constitute a terrorist fund under UAPA.

A Naxalite sympathiser in Chhattisgarh collects 'levy' (extortion money) from contractors and deposits it into a bank account controlled by a Maoist organisation; the accumulated amount in that account qualifies as a terrorist fund.

A businessman in Delhi purchases a commercial property using money wired to him by an ISIS-affiliated financier abroad, knowing its source; the money used for the purchase is a terrorist fund and the property is considered acquired through it.

Funds raised through fake charity drives by a designated terrorist organisation operating out of Jammu & Kashmir, ostensibly for flood relief but actually meant to pay its cadres and procure weapons, constitute a terrorist fund.

Cryptocurrency wallets controlled by an individual terrorist operating in Tamil Nadu and receiving Bitcoin payments from a foreign terrorist network for conducting reconnaissance activities represent a terrorist fund in digital form.
A trust registered in Hyderabad that funnels donations from overseas diaspora members to a banned organisation listed in the UAPA Schedule is holding and administering a terrorist fund.
what_it_covers: Money or assets collected, pooled, or transferred specifically to finance terrorist acts or terrorist organisations, regardless of whether the source of the money is itself lawful or unlawful.
Property — including cash, securities, real estate, or movable assets — acquired using funds channelled through or controlled by a terrorist organisation or individual terrorist.
Digital assets, cryptocurrency holdings, or hawala transfers that are used or intended to be used to sustain, resource, or advance terrorist activities in India or abroad.
Extortion proceeds, 'levies', or donations knowingly made to a banned terrorist organisation and held in any form pending deployment for terrorist purposes.
Foreign remittances or wire transfers routed through third-party accounts to ultimately fund recruitment, training, or operational planning of terrorist acts within India.
what_it_excludes: Legitimate funds held by a bona fide transferee who had no knowledge or reason to believe that the property was derived from or connected to any terrorist fund.
Funds raised and used exclusively for lawful charitable, humanitarian, or political purposes by organisations not designated or proscribed under the UAPA Schedule.

Assets that were initially derived from terrorist activity but have been lawfully seized, forfeited, or placed under a prohibitory order by a competent authority, as these are no longer in the possession or control of any terrorist entity.

General criminal proceeds unconnected to terrorism — for example, money derived from ordinary organised crime, drug trafficking, or corruption that has no nexus to a terrorist act, organisation, or activity.
Property held by government bodies, security forces, or the State arising from counter-terrorism operations, seizures, or confiscations under lawful authority.
