definitions.definition: 'terrorist gang' means any association, other than terrorist organisation, whether systematic or otherwise, which is concerned with, or involved in, terrorist act.
definitions.plain_english: A terrorist gang is any group of people — however loosely or informally organised — that is connected with or takes part in terrorist activities, but is not a formally listed terrorist organisation. Unlike a terrorist organisation, a terrorist gang does not need to be on a government schedule or list. The key requirement is simply that the group is involved in or associated with acts of terrorism in some way.
real_world_examples: A small cell of militants operating in a border district of Jammu & Kashmir who plan and carry out IED blasts on security convoys but are not affiliated with any Schedule-listed terrorist organisation like Lashkar-e-Taiba.

A group of radicalised individuals in an Indian city who collectively raise funds, procure weapons, and coordinate a targeted assassination of a public official, without belonging to a formally designated terrorist body.

An informal network of individuals in the Northeast who provide logistical support — safe houses, transportation, and communication — to perpetrators of terrorist acts, operating independently of any listed insurgent organisation.

A loosely organised gang in a coastal region that smuggles arms and explosives for use in terrorist attacks, without any formal membership structure or affiliation to a scheduled terrorist organisation.

A group of individuals recruited online who plan coordinated bomb blasts at public infrastructure in a metropolitan city, acting as an autonomous cell unconnected to any organisation listed in the UAPA Schedule.
what_it_covers: An informal cell of individuals with no formal name or charter who collectively plan or execute terrorist acts.
A loosely structured group that provides material support such as funds, shelter, or weapons to those committing terrorist acts, even if not directly involved in the act itself.
Any association — whether organised with clear hierarchy or completely ad hoc — that is concerned with terrorist activity, regardless of whether it has a formal membership list or manifesto.
A regional splinter group that has broken away from a listed terrorist organisation and operates independently while still engaging in terrorist acts.
what_it_excludes: Terrorist organisations formally listed in the Schedule to UAPA, which fall under the distinct definition of 'terrorist organisation' and are subject to separate provisions.
Individual terrorists acting alone without any association or combination with others, who are covered under the separate definition of 'individual terrorist'.
Unlawful associations that pursue activities such as sedition or threats to territorial integrity but are not involved in or concerned with terrorist acts as defined under Section 15 of UAPA.
Ordinary criminal gangs engaged in organised crime such as extortion or drug trafficking that have no connection to, or involvement in, any terrorist act.

definitions.definition: 'terrorist organisation' means an organisation listed in the Schedule or an organisation operating under the same name as an organisation so listed.
definitions.plain_english: A terrorist organisation under UAPA is any group that has been officially listed by the Indian government in the Schedule attached to the Act, or any group that uses the same name as such a listed organisation. The government has the power to add or remove organisations from this Schedule. Once listed, the organisation and activities associated with it attract serious criminal liability.
real_world_examples: Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT), which has been listed in the First Schedule of UAPA, is a terrorist organisation; any person who raises funds for LeT in India can be prosecuted under Section 17.
Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM), responsible for attacks such as the 2019 Pulwama attack, is listed in the Schedule; membership or support of JeM attracts criminal liability under Sections 20 and 38.

A newly formed militant group in Jammu & Kashmir that adopts the same name as a Schedule-listed banned outfit like Hizbul Mujahideen would automatically qualify as a terrorist organisation even before fresh listing, by virtue of operating under the same name.

The Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS/ISIL) is listed in the Schedule; a person in India who recruits individuals to join ISIS can be charged under Section 18 read with the terrorist organisation provisions.

The Communist Party of India (Maoist) is listed in the Schedule as a terrorist organisation; organising meetings, printing literature, or collecting funds in furtherance of its objectives constitutes an offence under UAPA.
what_it_covers: Any organisation explicitly named and listed in the First Schedule to the UAPA, such as Lashkar-e-Taiba, Jaish-e-Mohammed, or CPI (Maoist).
Any organisation that operates under the same name as a Schedule-listed organisation, even if it claims to be a distinct or newly formed entity.
Foreign organisations listed in the Schedule that operate or have members, supporters, or fund-raisers within Indian territory.
An organisation added to the Schedule by a Central Government notification under Section 35, from the date of such notification.
what_it_excludes: A 'terrorist gang', which is separately defined under UAPA as any association not listed in the Schedule that is involved in terrorist acts — it is expressly excluded from the definition of terrorist organisation.
An individual terrorist acting independently without being part of a Schedule-listed organisation, who is governed by separate provisions under the Act.

An unlawful association declared under Section 3 of UAPA that has not been separately listed in the Schedule as a terrorist organisation — it remains an unlawful association but not a terrorist organisation.
An organisation whose name is similar to but not the same as a Schedule-listed organisation; mere similarity of name does not bring it within the definition.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'terrorist organisation' determines the applicability of Sections 17, 20, 38, 39, and 40 of UAPA, which create distinct and severe offences for raising funds for, being a member of, supporting, or facilitating such an organisation, carrying enhanced punishments including imprisonment up to life. Designation as a terrorist organisation also enables the government to proceed under Sections 35 and 36 for listing or de-listing, and triggers stringent bail and procedural restrictions for accused persons.

definitions.definition: Training in terrorism refers to any instruction, drill, preparation, or indoctrination imparted at a camp or organised setting that equips individuals with skills, knowledge, tactics, or methods to commit or facilitate terrorist acts, including but not limited to weapons handling, explosives use, guerrilla tactics, surveillance techniques, or ideological radicalisation directed toward violent extremist ends.
definitions.plain_english: Training in terrorism means teaching or preparing people to carry out terrorist activities. This includes teaching someone how to use weapons, make bombs, conduct attacks, or follow extremist ideologies that promote violence. It is the kind of instruction given at secret camps run by terrorist groups to turn recruits into operatives capable of committing acts of terror.
real_world_examples: A militant outfit in Jammu & Kashmir sets up a forest camp where recruits are taught how to handle AK-47 rifles, lay improvised explosive devices, and evade security forces — this constitutes training in terrorism under Section 18A.

A Naxalite organisation in Chhattisgarh organises a remote jungle training camp where cadres are instructed in guerrilla warfare tactics, ambush techniques, and manufacturing of crude bombs to attack CRPF personnel.

An ISIS-affiliated sleeper cell in Hyderabad holds weekend sessions in a rented farmhouse where members are trained in knife attacks, surveillance of targets, and methods to avoid digital detection by intelligence agencies.

A Pakistan-based terrorist group conducts a cross-border training camp near the Line of Control where Indian recruits are given weapons training, grenade throwing practice, and lessons on bomb-making before being infiltrated into India.

A radical Islamist group in Kerala organises covert training sessions where youth are physically conditioned, taught combat techniques, and indoctrinated with violent jihadist ideology in preparation for planned attacks on public spaces.
what_it_covers: Physical combat and weapons handling sessions conducted at organised camps run by or for terrorist groups
Instruction in bomb-making, IED assembly, or use of explosives intended for committing terrorist acts
Ideological indoctrination at organised settings designed to prepare individuals to commit or support terrorist activities
Surveillance, evasion, and counter-intelligence training given to recruits at terrorist training facilities
Cyber-attack or digital sabotage training conducted in an organised manner to further terrorist objectives
what_it_excludes: Legitimate military or paramilitary training conducted by or under the authority of the armed forces of the Union or State police forces
Civilian self-defence classes, martial arts training, or sports shooting activities with no nexus to terrorist organisations or terrorist acts
Academic or research study of terrorism tactics in universities, think tanks, or intelligence training institutions for lawful counter-terrorism purposes
Protest organisation, civil disobedience training, or non-violent agitation preparation, even if related to unlawful associations, absent a link to terrorist acts
General physical fitness or outdoor survival training conducted by bona fide educational, scouting, or adventure organisations
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an activity qualifies as 'training in terrorism' directly determines criminal liability under Section 18A of UAPA, which mandates a minimum sentence of five years' imprisonment extendable to life along with a fine. Establishing this definition also triggers connected provisions relating to terrorist acts, terrorist organisations, and proceeds of terrorism, and enables courts to treat the organised camp as a terrorist activity warranting stringent bail conditions and special court procedures.

definitions.definition: In the context of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 'transfer' means any act of paying, delivering, conveying, assigning, or otherwise dealing with moneys, securities, credits, or property so as to pass control, title, or benefit from one person to another, including any arrangement that moves or encumbers property associated with an unlawful association or proceeds of terrorism.
definitions.plain_english: A 'transfer' is when someone moves money, property, or any valuable asset from their control to someone else's control. This includes handing over cash, moving funds between accounts, signing over property, or any other action that shifts ownership or use of something. Under UAPA, this word is used especially to prevent people from moving assets connected to terrorist organisations or unlawful associations.
real_world_examples: A hawala operator in Mumbai moves funds on behalf of a banned organisation by transferring equivalent amounts through informal channels to operatives in another state, constituting a prohibited transfer under UAPA.

A sympathiser of a declared unlawful association in Jammu & Kashmir transfers ownership of a plot of land to a family member of an active member of the organisation to shield the asset from attachment by investigating authorities.

A bank account holder in Hyderabad, despite receiving a prohibitory order under Section 7, transfers credits from his account to a third-party account linked to a terrorist gang, violating the prohibition on transfer of funds.

A person in Delhi, aware that certain securities held by him represent proceeds of terrorism, sells and delivers those securities to a buyer before the Designated Authority can confirm the attachment order, thereby completing an illegal transfer.

A trust administrator in Chennai, whose trust funds have been frozen under a UAPA order, attempts to transfer the beneficial interest in the trust assets to a shell company to circumvent the prohibitory order issued by the Central Government.
what_it_covers: Payment or delivery of moneys, securities, or credits from one person to another in violation of a prohibitory order issued under Section 7.
Assignment or conveyance of immovable or movable property that represents proceeds of terrorism, in contravention of a seizure or attachment order under Section 25.
Any informal or formal arrangement — including hawala, benami transactions, or gift deeds — through which control or benefit of assets linked to an unlawful association is passed to another party.
Electronic or digital transfer of funds, including bank wire transfers, UPI transactions, or cryptocurrency movements, involving property subject to UAPA proceedings.
Endorsement, pledging, or hypothecation of securities or credits that effectively shifts beneficial ownership away from the person against whom a prohibitory or attachment order has been made.
what_it_excludes: Transfers made in full compliance with and under written authorisation of the Central Government as expressly permitted by a prohibitory order under Section 7.
Bona fide transfers completed before the issuance and service of any prohibitory or attachment order, where the transferee had no knowledge of the association or proceedings.

Court-directed transfers or distributions of property that are made pursuant to a judicial order of the District Judge or other competent court in the course of established legal proceedings under the Act.
Ordinary commercial transactions involving property that has no nexus whatsoever to an unlawful association, terrorist organisation, or proceeds of terrorism.
Internal accounting entries or ledger adjustments within the same legal entity that do not result in any actual movement of assets or change in beneficial ownership.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act constitutes a 'transfer' determines whether a person is criminally liable under Section 11 for contravening a prohibitory order (punishable with up to three years' imprisonment and fine) or whether an attachment under Section 25 has been unlawfully defeated, triggering forfeiture proceedings and additional penalties; establishing that a transfer occurred is thus central to both the prohibition regime and the proceeds-of-terrorism framework under UAPA.

definitions.definition: 'Tribunal' means the Tribunal constituted under section 5.
definitions.plain_english: The Tribunal under UAPA is a special judicial body set up under Section 5 of the Act to review and confirm (or revoke) the government's decision to ban an organisation as 'unlawful'. It is headed by a High Court judge and acts as an independent check on the Central Government's power to declare associations unlawful. Without the Tribunal's confirmation, a ban on an organisation cannot remain in force beyond a certain period.
real_world_examples: When the Central Government issued a notification declaring the Students Islamic Movement of India (SIMI) as an unlawful association, the matter was referred to the UAPA Tribunal (headed by a sitting or retired High Court judge) to examine the evidence and confirm or revoke the ban.

After the government banned the Popular Front of India (PFI) in September 2022, the case was placed before the Tribunal constituted under Section 5 of UAPA, which reviewed the grounds and materials submitted by the government to decide whether the ban should be confirmed.

A Kashmiri separatist organisation declared unlawful by the Central Government had the opportunity to appear before the Tribunal and present its case; the Tribunal then adjudicated whether the notification banning the organisation should continue.

When Jamaat-ul-Mujahideen Bangladesh's activities were flagged in India and the government declared it unlawful, the Tribunal under Section 5 was constituted to independently assess the materials and decide on the legality and continuation of the ban.

In a case where a northeastern insurgent group was declared an unlawful association, its representatives were allowed to appear before the Tribunal constituted under Section 5 to contest the government notification, ensuring a quasi-judicial safeguard against arbitrary executive action.
what_it_covers: The judicial body constituted under Section 5 of UAPA, presided over by a sitting or retired judge of a High Court, tasked with reviewing government notifications declaring associations as unlawful.
The forum before which a banned organisation or association may appear to contest the Central Government's declaration of it as an unlawful association.

The authority empowered to confirm, modify, or revoke a notification issued by the Central Government under Section 3 declaring an association to be unlawful, thereby giving legal finality to the ban.
The Tribunal's proceedings and orders made in the course of reviewing whether an association rightly qualifies as an 'unlawful association' under the Act.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary criminal courts or Special Courts constituted under Section 11 of UAPA or Section 21 of the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008, which are defined separately as 'court' under Section 2.
Review Committees or administrative bodies set up under other statutes (such as under the National Security Act or the Foreigners Act), which are not the Tribunal under Section 5 of UAPA.
Civil courts, consumer forums, or any other adjudicatory body not specifically constituted under Section 5 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
The 'Designated Authority' (a senior government officer) who performs separate functions under the Act such as granting sanction for prosecution, as that is a distinct role from the Tribunal.
definitions.why_it_matters: The Tribunal is the sole body empowered to confirm the continued operation of a government notification declaring an association unlawful; without the Tribunal's confirmation, a ban under Section 3 cannot remain legally valid beyond the statutory review period. Membership, support, or funding of an association confirmed as unlawful by the Tribunal triggers serious criminal liability under Sections 10, 11, and 13 of UAPA, including imprisonment, making the Tribunal's decision a pivotal gateway to criminal prosecution.

definitions.definition: 'Tribunal' means the Tribunal constituted under section 5.
definitions.plain_english: The Tribunal is a special adjudicatory body set up under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act specifically to review whether an association declared unlawful by the Central Government should continue to be treated as such. It is not a regular court but a dedicated quasi-judicial forum established under Section 5 of UAPA. Its role is to confirm, modify, or set aside the government's notification declaring an organisation unlawful.
real_world_examples: When the Central Government declared the Popular Front of India (PFI) as an unlawful association in 2022, the matter was referred to the Tribunal constituted under Section 5 of UAPA to adjudicate whether sufficient cause existed to confirm the ban.

After the Government of India declared the Students Islamic Movement of India (SIMI) as an unlawful association, the UAPA Tribunal held hearings, examined evidence, and passed an order confirming the ban, which was later challenged in the High Court.

The Tribunal proceedings under Section 4 of UAPA require affected associations to be given an opportunity to be heard before the Tribunal decides whether to confirm the declaration of unlawfulness made against them.

Under Section 9 of UAPA, an office-bearer of an organisation declared unlawful may appear before the Tribunal to contest the notification and present evidence that the association does not engage in unlawful activities.

In a case where a regional separatist group was notified as an unlawful association, the Tribunal examined classified intelligence reports and witness depositions over several sittings before issuing its final order under Section 5 of UAPA.
what_it_covers: The body constituted by the Central Government under Section 5 of UAPA, presided over by a Judge of a High Court, to adjudicate the legality and continuance of a notification declaring an association unlawful.

Proceedings under Section 4 of UAPA where the Tribunal reviews evidence placed by the Central Government and hears representations from the concerned association before confirming or setting aside a ban.
Orders passed by the Tribunal under Section 9 of UAPA that are binding on all parties and which determine the legal status of an association as unlawful for the duration specified under the Act.
Hearings conducted by the Tribunal in which classified or sensitive government information may be examined in camera, and where the Tribunal may call for additional evidence or witnesses.
what_it_excludes: Ordinary criminal courts or sessions courts that try offences under UAPA — these are covered under the definition of 'court' in Section 2, not 'Tribunal'.

Special Courts constituted under Section 11 of UAPA or under Section 21 of the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008, which deal with prosecution of terrorist offences rather than adjudication of unlawful association status.
Review Committees constituted under UAPA for other purposes, which are distinct bodies and do not perform the adjudicatory function of confirming or setting aside unlawful association notifications.
High Courts or the Supreme Court exercising appellate or writ jurisdiction over Tribunal orders — they are superior constitutional courts, not the Tribunal itself.
Administrative or executive bodies of the Central Government or State Government that issue the initial notification declaring an association as unlawful under Section 3.
definitions.why_it_matters: The existence and decision of the Tribunal is a mandatory procedural safeguard: under Section 4 of UAPA, a notification declaring an association unlawful lapses unless confirmed by the Tribunal, meaning the entire legal consequence of treating an organisation as unlawful — including criminal liability of members under Section 10 and seizure of property — depends on the Tribunal's confirmation. Without a valid Tribunal order, prosecutions and prohibitory actions premised on the unlawful status of the association may be legally unsustainable.

definitions.definition: "trust" means any body registered under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 (2 of 1882) or any other State Act governing the registration of trusts.
definitions.plain_english: A 'trust' under UAPA refers to a formally registered charitable, religious, or private trust that has been set up and enrolled under the Indian Trusts Act or a similar state-level law. It is treated as a legal entity that can commit offences, and its officers and settlors can be held personally responsible for those offences. The law uses this definition to ensure that terrorist financing or unlawful activities carried out through trust structures can be prosecuted.
real_world_examples: A registered charitable trust in Maharashtra, set up under the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, that is found to be channelling donations to a banned terrorist organisation — it falls squarely within this definition and its trustees can be prosecuted under UAPA.

A religious trust registered under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 in Uttar Pradesh whose accounts are used to launder terrorist funds collected from overseas — the trust and its settlor are both liable under Sections 22B and 22C.

A welfare trust registered in Tamil Nadu under the Tamil Nadu Public Trusts Act that knowingly provides logistical support (safe houses, vehicles) to members of an unlawful association — the managing trustees can be charged as if personally guilty of the offence.

A private family trust registered under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 in Delhi whose trustee, with the knowledge of other officers, transfers proceeds of terrorism to operatives abroad — both the trust entity and the responsible officers face imprisonment of not less than seven years under Section 22C.

An educational trust registered in Kerala that is used as a front to recruit individuals for terrorist training camps — the promoter and every officer in charge at the time of the offence are deemed guilty under Section 22B.
what_it_covers: Any trust registered under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 at the central level.
Any trust registered under a State Act governing trust registration, such as the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act or the Tamil Nadu Public Trusts Act.
A trust entity whose settlor, trustees, managers, secretaries, or other officers are involved in the commission of an offence under UAPA — all such persons are deemed guilty along with the trust.
A trust that commits an offence through the consent, connivance, or neglect of any of its office-bearers, making each such officer independently liable.
A trust used as a vehicle to hold, transfer, or manage funds, economic resources, or property connected to terrorist activity.
what_it_excludes: Unregistered or informal trust arrangements that have not been enrolled under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 or any applicable State Act — such bodies do not fall within this statutory definition.
Companies incorporated under the Companies Act, which are separately defined and governed under a distinct provision (Section 22A/22C) as a 'company', not a 'trust'.
Societies registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 or State equivalents, which are separately defined as a 'society' and treated as a distinct category from 'trust' under Section 22B.

Ex officio members of a trust's governing board who represent the interests of the Central or State Government or a statutory authority — they are excluded from the definition of 'director' and shielded from automatic liability.

A person who proves that the offence was committed without their knowledge or that they exercised reasonable care to prevent it — such a person is excluded from punishment even if they fall within the trust's management structure.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'trust' under this definition determines whether UAPA's collective criminal liability provisions (Sections 22B and 22C) can be invoked — triggering mandatory minimum imprisonment of seven years up to life and fines between five and ten crore rupees for every responsible officer. Without this classification, individual officers and the settlor could not be automatically deemed guilty for offences committed by the trust entity.

definitions.definition: The term 'unity' is not separately defined in the Act but is used in Section 15 as a foundational constitutional value whose threatened disruption constitutes a terrorist act; it refers to the oneness and indivisibility of India as a single sovereign nation, encompassing the political, territorial, and social cohesion of the Indian State, such that any act intended or likely to threaten this oneness — whether through violence, disruption, or coercion — attracts liability under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: Unity here means keeping India together as one undivided country without internal fragmentation or break-up driven by violence or terror. It is the idea that all parts of India — its states, regions, and people — remain bound together under one national identity and government. Any violent act or threat that tries to split this togetherness or cause different parts of India to break away is treated as a terrorist act under UAPA.
real_world_examples: A separatist armed group operating in the Northeast India plants bombs in government buildings and issues statements demanding a separate independent nation carved out of Indian territory — this act threatens the unity of India and constitutes a terrorist act under Section 15.

An organisation based in Pakistan funds and trains individuals to orchestrate simultaneous blasts in multiple Indian cities with the stated goal of inspiring ethnic communities to declare independence from India — directly threatening India's unity.

A Naxal outfit systematically attacks railway infrastructure, government offices, and security personnel in central India to create liberated zones that reject Indian state authority, intending to territorially fragment the nation — threatening India's unity.

Militants in Jammu & Kashmir systematically assassinate local political leaders and civil servants, distribute propaganda calling for secession from India, and coerce local populations to reject Indian governance structures — threatening India's unity as contemplated under Section 15.

A foreign-backed cyber group launches coordinated attacks on national communication infrastructure combined with disinformation campaigns aimed at inflaming regional identities to the point of armed separatism — threatening the unity of India through non-conventional means covered under Section 15.
what_it_covers: Acts of violence or terror aimed at breaking India into separate political entities or carving out independent states from Indian territory
Coercive campaigns using bombs, firearms, or other lethal means that are intended to weaken the central bond between Indian states and the Union
Propaganda-backed armed movements that seek to fragment the national identity by inciting regional or ethnic communities to reject Indian sovereignty through force
Attacks on constitutional authority or public functionaries carried out with the goal of dismantling the unified governance structure of India
Foreign-sponsored or domestically-organised terrorist activity whose declared or inferable objective is to cause India to lose cohesion as a single political unit
what_it_excludes: Lawful political movements, democratic protests, or peaceful demands for greater autonomy or statehood that do not involve violence or terror
Academic, journalistic, or policy discussions advocating federalism, regional rights, or constitutional restructuring without any element of violence or coercion
Civil unrest, riots, or communal violence that, while serious criminal acts, are not directed at breaking up India as a nation and lack the requisite intent to threaten unity
Ordinary criminal offences such as robbery, murder, or kidnapping that have no connection to the goal of fragmenting or destabilising the Indian State
Diplomatic or legal challenges by State Governments against Union policies through constitutional mechanisms, which are entirely outside the ambit of this definition
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act is found to 'threaten the unity of India' is one of the primary threshold conditions under Section 15 that transforms an ordinary criminal act into a terrorist act, thereby attracting the far more stringent penalties, extended pre-trial detention, special court procedures, and reverse burden-of-proof provisions under UAPA. If this threshold is met, the accused faces prosecution under UAPA rather than ordinary penal law, with significantly reduced bail entitlements and enhanced sentencing including the possibility of death penalty for certain forms of the offence.

definitions.definition: 'Unlawful activity', in relation to an individual or association, means any action taken by such individual or association (whether by committing an act or by words, either spoken or written, or by signs or by visible representation or otherwise),— which is intended, or supports any claim, to bring about, on any ground whatsoever, the cession of a part of the territory of India or the secession of a part of the territory of India from the Union, or which incites any individual or group of individuals to bring about such cession or secession; or which disclaims, questions, disrupts or is intended to disrupt the sovereignty and territorial integrity of India; or which causes or is intended to cause disaffection against India.
definitions.plain_english: Unlawful activity refers to any action — whether through deeds, speech, writing, symbols, or other visible means — by a person or group that promotes the breaking away of any part of India from the country, challenges India's sovereignty or territorial wholeness, or stirs up hatred or disloyalty against India. It does not matter what reason or ground is put forward to justify such action. Both direct acts and incitement of others to do such things are covered.
real_world_examples: A political activist in Manipur publicly distributing pamphlets demanding that the state secede from India and form an independent nation, inciting locals to support armed separatist groups.

A social media influencer based in Punjab posting videos questioning the legitimacy of India's sovereignty over Jammu & Kashmir and urging followers to support a foreign country's territorial claim over the region.

A registered association in Tamil Nadu passing resolutions at public meetings that openly disclaim India's authority over certain border territories and advocate for their cession to a neighbouring country.

A speaker at a public rally in Hyderabad delivering speeches intended to cause widespread disaffection against the Indian state by portraying the Government of India as an illegitimate occupying force.

An organisation in West Bengal circulating written material supporting a secessionist movement in North-East India, advising sympathisers on how to assist separatist factions in disrupting the territorial integrity of India.

An individual using sign-based protests and visible banners at a public venue in Delhi explicitly endorsing demands by a foreign-backed group for the fragmentation of Indian territory along religious or linguistic lines.
what_it_covers: Written or spoken words by an individual that support claims for the cession or secession of any part of Indian territory on any ground whatsoever.
Actions or gestures (including signs and visible representations) by an association that are intended to disrupt the sovereignty or territorial integrity of India.
Incitement by any person or group directed at others to bring about secession or cession of Indian territory, even if the person does not directly commit the act.
Any conduct — whether an overt act or expression — that causes or is intended to cause disaffection against India as a nation.

definitions.definition: "Unlawful association" means any association which has for its object any unlawful activity, or which encourages or aids persons to undertake any unlawful activity, or of which the members undertake such activity; or which has for its object any activity which is punishable under section 153A or section 153B of the Indian Penal Code, or which encourages or aids persons to undertake any such activity, or of which the members undertake any such activity: Provided that nothing contained in sub-clause (ii) shall apply to the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
definitions.plain_english: An unlawful association is any group or organisation whose goal is to carry out activities that threaten India's territorial integrity, sovereignty, or promote enmity between communities. It also includes groups that help or encourage their members to do such things. Once declared unlawful by the Central Government, being a member of or supporting such a group becomes a punishable offence.
real_world_examples: An organisation based in Punjab that publicly campaigns for a separate Khalistan state and recruits members to agitate for secession from India would qualify as an unlawful association under the first limb of the definition.

A student group in a central university that distributes pamphlets denying India's sovereignty over Jammu and Kashmir and organises protests calling for its cession to a foreign country could be declared an unlawful association.

An organisation that systematically publishes hate literature promoting enmity between Hindus and Muslims on grounds of religion, thereby committing acts punishable under Section 153A IPC, would fall under the second limb of the definition.

A registered NGO that covertly funds and logistically aids individuals to disrupt the territorial integrity of India, even if its stated charitable objects are benign, could be declared an unlawful association based on the activities its members undertake.

A social media collective that coordinates and incites communal violence between scheduled caste and upper caste communities in multiple states, with conduct attracting Section 153B IPC, may be declared an unlawful association.

A political front organisation that operates as a mouthpiece for a banned separatist movement, encouraging disaffection against India through speeches and publications, can be classified as an unlawful association even if it has not itself been previously proscribed.
what_it_covers: Any association whose primary or incidental object is to bring about cession or secession of any part of Indian territory, whether by direct action or by supporting individuals who pursue such goals.
Organisations that do not themselves commit unlawful acts but actively encourage, aid, or facilitate their members or third parties to undertake unlawful activity as defined under the Act.

Groups whose members collectively undertake activities punishable under Section 153A (promoting enmity between groups) or Section 153B (imputations prejudicial to national integration) of the Indian Penal Code.

An association that disclaims or questions the sovereignty and territorial integrity of India through its publications, meetings, or coordinated conduct, even if individual acts are not yet prosecuted.
A body that causes or intends to cause disaffection against India through systematic propaganda, fundraising, or recruitment drives conducted by or for the association.
what_it_excludes: A legitimate political party or civil society organisation that peacefully advocates for constitutional amendments or greater autonomy within the framework of the Indian Constitution, provided it does not promote secession or cession.
Academic institutions, research bodies, or think tanks that study separatist movements or publish critical analysis of government policy without encouraging or aiding unlawful activity.

Religious or cultural organisations operating lawfully within India whose members may individually hold dissenting views but whose organisational objects and collective activities do not involve any unlawful activity under the Act.

Terrorist organisations as such, which are separately defined and governed under the Schedule and sections 35–40 of UAPA, and are distinct from the category of 'unlawful association' though overlap is possible.

Associations operating solely in Jammu and Kashmir whose activities would only attract the second limb of the definition (Sections 153A/153B IPC), in view of the express proviso excluding that State from that sub-clause.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as an 'unlawful association' is the threshold trigger for the Central Government's power under Section 3 to issue a proscription notification, and once declared unlawful, membership, financial support, and management of such association attract criminal penalties under Sections 10, 11, and 13 of UAPA, including imprisonment; additionally, Sections 7 and 8 enable seizure and forfeiture of the association's funds and property, while Section 4 imposes liability for use of funds contributed to it.

definitions.definition: Firearms possessed or carried without a valid licence as required under applicable law, including the Arms Act, 1959. In the context of Section 10 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 'unlicensed firearms' refers to any firearm held by a member or associate of an unlawful association for which the possessor does not hold a lawful licence or authorisation under prevailing Indian firearms legislation.
definitions.plain_english: Unlicensed firearms are guns or weapons that someone possesses or uses without having the legal government-issued permission (licence) required to own or carry them. In simple terms, if a person has a pistol, rifle, or any other firearm that is not registered or permitted under the law, it is considered 'unlicensed.' Under UAPA, being a member of a banned organisation and also having such illegal firearms significantly increases the criminal punishment.
real_world_examples: A member of a banned terrorist organisation in Jammu & Kashmir is found carrying an AK-47 rifle with no Arms Act licence — this constitutes possession of unlicensed firearms under Section 10 of UAPA.

A Naxalite cadre in Chhattisgarh, declared part of an unlawful association, is apprehended with a country-made pistol (katta) for which no licence exists, triggering the aggravated penalty provisions under Section 10(b).

In a police raid on a suspected sleeper cell of a notified terrorist organisation in Hyderabad, multiple unregistered revolvers and ammunition are recovered from members who possess no firearms licences under the Arms Act, 1959.

Security forces in Manipur arrest an operative of a proscribed insurgent group found with two unlicensed semi-automatic weapons; since a civilian is killed in the operation, the death penalty or life imprisonment becomes applicable under Section 10(b)(i).

A fundraiser for a declared unlawful association in Punjab is discovered to have two unlicensed shotguns at his premises; although he has not personally caused any violence, the possession itself along with his association membership attracts enhanced liability under Section 10.
what_it_covers: Any firearm (pistol, revolver, rifle, shotgun, carbine) possessed by a member of a notified unlawful association without a valid Arms Act licence.
Country-made or improvised firearms (e.g., 'katta') held by individuals associated with banned organisations, for which no lawful authorisation exists.
Firearms obtained through illegal channels (smuggling, theft from security forces) and held by operatives of unlawful associations without any licence or government permit.
Foreign-origin weapons such as AK-series rifles or pistols possessed by members of proscribed groups operating in insurgency-affected regions without any valid Indian licence.
Firearms whose licence has expired, been revoked, or was never obtained, held by persons actively participating in or aiding an unlawful association.
what_it_excludes: Firearms held by serving members of the armed forces, police, or paramilitary forces in their official capacity, as such possession is authorised by law.

Licensed firearms legally held by civilians under a valid Arms Act licence, even if those individuals are incidentally associated with persons connected to an unlawful association, provided the licence is current and lawful.
Antique or deactivated firearms that are legally exempted from licence requirements under the Arms Act, 1959, and are not functional or capable of causing harm.
Air guns and certain low-calibre weapons specifically exempted from licensing requirements under the Arms Act, 1959, and related rules.
Firearms held by authorised arms dealers or gunsmiths under valid dealer licences, even if temporarily in their possession without individual user licences.
definitions.why_it_matters: The presence of unlicensed firearms in the hands of a member of an unlawful association directly elevates the offence under Section 10 from a basic membership penalty (up to two years) to a potentially capital offence punishable by death or life imprisonment if the act results in loss of human life, or a minimum of five years up to life imprisonment in other cases. This element is a statutory aggravating factor that transforms a relatively minor association offence into one of the most serious offences under UAPA.

definitions.definition: A 'witness' under this Act means any person who is a witness in proceedings under the Act, including proceedings before the Tribunal or any court, and whose testimony, evidence, or participation in such proceedings may expose them or persons in whom they are interested to threats, violence, wrongful restraint, or wrongful confinement as contemplated under Section 22.
definitions.plain_english: A witness is any person who gives or is expected to give evidence or testimony in a legal case or inquiry under the UAPA. This includes people called to testify before courts or tribunals dealing with unlawful activities or terrorist offences. The law specifically protects such persons and those close to them from threats, intimidation, or physical harm intended to influence or suppress their testimony.
real_world_examples: A resident of a locality in Kashmir who witnessed a terrorist attack and is called to depose before the NIA Special Court as a prosecution witness in a UAPA trial.

A member of the public who saw members of a banned organisation distributing inflammatory material and is summoned to appear before the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Tribunal constituted under Section 5.
A former associate of a designated terrorist organisation who turns approver and provides testimony before a sessions court in Mumbai in a UAPA case, and receives threats to withdraw his evidence.

A journalist who documented the activities of an unlawful association and is subpoenaed as a witness in proceedings before the District Judge under Section 8, and subsequently faces intimidation from members of that association.
A police constable who is a material witness in a UAPA case involving a terrorist gang operating in Jharkhand and is threatened by associates of the accused to prevent him from deposing.
A neighbour who testifies about suspicious activities at a notified place under Section 8 and whose family members are threatened with physical harm to coerce him into retracting his statement.
what_it_covers: A person who has been summoned to give oral or written evidence in any proceeding before the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Tribunal under Section 5 of the Act.
A person who is a witness in a criminal trial or inquiry before any court dealing with offences under the UAPA, including NIA Special Courts.

A person who has already deposed or is about to depose in proceedings relating to an unlawful association or terrorist act, and who is subjected to threats or physical restraint to influence their testimony.
Any person who is a potential witness expected to give evidence in future proceedings under the Act and who is threatened with violence on that account.
A witness's family members or close associates who are threatened or harmed as a means of coercing the witness, who are covered as persons 'in whom the witness may be interested.'
what_it_excludes: An accused person or suspect in a UAPA case who is not appearing or summoned in the capacity of a witness but as a party to the proceedings.
A person who has no connection to any proceedings under the UAPA and is threatened for reasons entirely unrelated to any such case or inquiry.
Persons who merely possess knowledge of relevant facts but have not been summoned, identified, or recognised as witnesses in any pending or anticipated proceedings under the Act.
Legal representatives, advocates, or counsel appearing in UAPA proceedings, who are not 'witnesses' in the evidentiary sense and whose protection is governed by separate provisions.
Investigators or police officers acting in their official investigative capacity, who are not functioning as witnesses in the proceedings in question.

definitions.definition: Wrongful confinement, as used in Section 22 of the UAPA, refers to the act of unlawfully restraining or confining a witness or any person in whom such witness may be interested, so as to prevent that witness from freely participating in a judicial or investigative proceeding, where such confinement is carried out with the intent to intimidate, coerce, or obstruct the course of justice.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongful confinement means illegally locking up, trapping, or physically restricting a witness or someone close to them so that the witness cannot move freely or testify. This is done to intimidate the witness or stop them from giving evidence. It is a form of obstruction of justice under the UAPA and is treated as a serious criminal offence.
real_world_examples: Members of a banned terrorist organisation in Jammu & Kashmir lock a key prosecution witness inside a room in their house for several days before a scheduled court hearing to prevent the witness from testifying against their associates.

Sympathisers of an unlawful association in Punjab abduct and confine the spouse of a protected witness in a hideout, intending to pressure the witness into retracting their deposition before a UAPA tribunal.

In a Naxal-affected district of Chhattisgarh, armed cadres of a proscribed organisation detain a villager who witnessed an IED attack and keep them confined in a forest camp so they cannot approach the investigating officer or appear before the court.

A network of accused persons in a UAPA terror-financing case in Mumbai unlawfully confine the minor child of a witness in an apartment, signalling to the witness that harm will follow unless the witness refuses to depose, constituting wrongful confinement of a person in whom the witness is interested.

In Delhi, handlers of a terrorist gang hold a witness's elderly parent against their will inside a private premises for 48 hours immediately before a critical bail hearing, coercing the witness to remain absent from the proceedings.

what_it_excludes: Lawful custody or detention of a witness ordered by a competent court or authority under applicable law, such as a witness protection order or remand.

Covers: Physically locking a witness inside a building, room, or enclosed space without lawful authority to prevent testimony.; Unlawfully detaining or confining any person — such as a family member, friend, or associate — in whom the witness has an interest, as a means of coercing or threatening the witness.; Any act of restricting the free movement of a witness or a related person carried out with the intent to intimidate or obstruct judicial or investigative proceedings under the UAPA.; Confinement carried out by members, promoters, or office-bearers of an unlawful association or terrorist organisation to suppress witness testimony.; Indirect confinement such as holding a witness captive in an isolated location under armed guard to ensure non-appearance before a court or tribunal.

Excludes: Lawful custody or detention of a witness ordered by a competent court or authority under applicable law, such as a witness protection order or remand.; Mere persuasion or verbal requests directed at a witness to avoid appearing in court, which do not involve any physical restraint or confinement.; Confinement of a person who has no connection whatsoever to a witness or any ongoing judicial or investigative proceeding under the UAPA.; Voluntary isolation or self-imposed restriction of movement by a witness, not induced by any external unlawful act of another person.; Detention of a witness by law enforcement agencies acting within the scope of their legal powers under the Code of Criminal Procedure or the UAPA itself.

Why it matters: If wrongful confinement is established under Section 22, the offender faces imprisonment of up to three years along with a fine, making it a cognizable offence that directly triggers arrest powers and criminal prosecution. The provision is critical for protecting witnesses in UAPA cases and ensuring that terrorist or unlawful associations cannot suppress evidence by physically restraining witnesses or those connected to them.

definitions.definition: Wrongful restraint, as used in Section 22 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, refers to the act of illegally preventing or obstructing a witness, or any person in whom such witness may be interested, from moving freely or proceeding as they otherwise would, without lawful justification, with the intent to intimidate or interfere with the witness in relation to any proceeding or investigation under the Act.
definitions.plain_english: Wrongful restraint means illegally stopping or blocking a witness or someone close to them from moving or going where they want to go. It does not involve physically locking someone up, but rather preventing their free movement through force, threat, or unlawful means. This is done with the purpose of pressuring, intimidating, or silencing the witness in a terrorism-related case.
real_world_examples: A group of individuals affiliated with a banned terrorist organisation physically blocks a witness's car on a highway in Jammu & Kashmir, preventing them from reaching the National Investigation Agency office to record their statement, thereby restraining the witness without legal authority.

Sympathisers of an accused under UAPA surround a witness's home in Hyderabad and prevent family members from leaving the house, intending to pressure the witness to withdraw their testimony in an ongoing UAPA trial.

Armed associates of a terrorist gang in Manipur intercept a witness at a bus stand, physically hold them back and threaten them, preventing the witness from travelling to another city to depose before the Designated Court.

In Mumbai, persons linked to an unlawful association forcibly detain the brother of a key prosecution witness in a parking lot, blocking his vehicle and refusing to let him leave, intending to compel the witness to remain silent or turn hostile.

Members of a proscribed organisation in Uttar Pradesh station themselves outside the residence of a witness, preventing them from stepping out to attend a court hearing in a terrorism financing case under UAPA, thereby wrongfully restraining their movement.
what_it_covers: Physically blocking a witness or a person of interest to the witness from moving from one place to another without lawful justification.
Surrounding or intercepting a witness's family member to prevent their free movement as a means of pressuring the witness in a UAPA proceeding.
Using force, threat of force, or unlawful assembly to stop a witness from travelling to a court, NIA office, or any investigative authority.
Stationing armed individuals or a group outside a witness's residence to obstruct their exit with intent to interfere with their testimony.
Detaining a vehicle or physically holding back any person in whom the witness has a personal interest, to coerce the witness indirectly.
what_it_excludes: Lawful restraint carried out by police or security forces under a valid legal authority, warrant, or order of a competent court or authority.
Wrongful confinement, which involves enclosing a person within defined boundaries on all sides and is a distinct, more severe offence also referenced in Section 22.
Verbal threats or mere surveillance of a witness without any actual physical obstruction of their movement, which may fall under a different limb of Section 22.
Civil disputes or contractual obligations that incidentally restrict a person's movement, as these lack the criminal intent and unlawful character required under Section 22.
Restraint carried out by persons with no connection to a witness or to any proceeding under the UAPA, which would fall under general criminal law rather than this provision.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an act qualifies as wrongful restraint under Section 22 of UAPA determines whether the perpetrator is liable for punishment of up to three years of imprisonment and a fine, as opposed to a lesser offence under the Indian Penal Code; it directly triggers prosecution for obstruction of justice in terrorism-related proceedings and strengthens witness protection mechanisms under the Act.
